#8213. 8 Wild Fish and Game Recipes to Recreate the First Thanksgiving Dinner

Early Black Friday deals are here — Shop hunting gear, fishing tackle, optics, and more!

Published Nov 25, 2026 3:00 PM EST

The hottest fishing news, tips, and tactics

Turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce, pumpkin pie, and football. In America, that’s usually what’s on the menu on the fourth Thursday in November. But in the fall of 1621, the original Thanksgiving meal didn’t resemble this in the slightest. The Pilgrims at Plymouth Plantation had a lot to be thankful for. The Wampanoag helped them survive the previous winter and harvest plenty of food over the summer. The two groups decided to come together and celebrate this for a few days with a feast, during which they ate a mix of wild fish and game. Here is an excerpt from one of two firsthand accounts from a man named Edward Winslow:

“Our harvest being gotten in, our governor sent four men on fowling, that so we might after a special manner rejoice together after we had gathered the fruit of our labors. They four in one day killed as much fowl as, with a little help beside, served the company almost a week. At which time, amongst other recreations, we exercised our arms, many of the Indians coming amongst us, and among the rest their greatest king Massasoit, with some ninety men, whom for three days we entertained and feasted, and they went out and killed five deer, which they brought to the plantation and bestowed on our governor, and upon the captain and others.”

That sounds a little more like deer camp than grandma’s house. Along with a pile of venison and week’s supply of fowl, it’s not out of the question to assume there were also dried fruits, berries, nuts, fish, and shellfish at the feast. Being that most of these things are available to hunters and anglers, we took a deep dive into some of our favorite recipes. In the spirit of that original Thanksgiving meal, here are eight ways to bring back some wild game to the table this season.

The Wampanoag showed the colonists a lot ways to grow and keep food, but neither group had access to refrigeration. Instead, things like berries and other fruit had to be eaten fresh or preserved. The most likely way they would have done this is by drying, but there’s another way to preserve fruit without refrigeration. Canning has been done for generations, and it’s still a perfect way to preserve wild berries for months. The pilgrims wouldn’t have had the sugar for this wild black raspberry jam recipe, but it still goes good with butter and toast, on a leftover turkey sandwich, or even some acorn-flour pancakes.

Today lobsters and other shellfish are considered delicacies, but 400 years ago, they were a staple. The Atlantic coastline provided Wampanoag and the colonists with clams, mussels, and lobster. But there’s also another crustacean, readily available in freshwater, that’s just as worthy of dipping in clarified butter: the crayfish. Here’s a classic crayfish etouffee to serve alongside the main course.

In a heavy-bottomed pan, melt the butter and add the flour. You are going to make a roux: over medium heat, stir the roux until it darkens to the color of peanut butter (about 20 minutes). Add the onions, celery, and green peppers, stirring to combine. Add the garlic, tomato paste, and Worcestershire. Stir for a couple of minutes. Pour in the stock and the cooked crayfish tail meat. Stir for a few minutes until the roux in well incorporated into the stock and it starts to boil. Turn the heat down to a simmer, and add the Cajun seasoning. Then simmer for about 20 minutes until the etouffee thickens. Serve over wild rice or plain white rice. If you like yours a little hotter, add Crystal hot sauce or your favorite hot sauce.

In the first sentence of the Winslow account, there’s a mention of fowl:

“Our harvest being gotten in, our governor sent four men on fowling, that so we might after a special manner rejoice together after we had gathered the fruit of our labors.”

Turkey is considered fowl, but the first thanksgiving probably included waterfowl instead. Ducks and geese would have been easier for the settlers and the Wampanoag to catch and cook. They are also more plentiful in the wild. The birds were most likely roasted over a fire. Spit roasting a whole bird is an involved process, and most will opt for an oven instead, given a chance. If you’re thinking about swapping duck for a turkey this year, this wild duck and squash curry is an excellent place to start.

Another bird readily available in the 17th century was the passenger pigeon. When populations were at their peak, it is said that flocks were so thick they would black out the sky. Unfortunately, this didn’t last. Due to heavy market hunting and habitat loss, the passenger pigeon is now extinct. A similar bird (though not closely related) is the mourning dove. In fact, one of the last living wild passenger pigeons was found roosting with mourning doves.

A classic popper recipe will work with doves and most other upland birds (and it also pairs well with football). But most dove hunters already have that recipe figured out. Instead, here’s a flaky cheese and pepper dove roll recipe that’s sure to please.

Fish played a big part in the colonist’s lives. They were loaned money to start the colony, and they planned to pay some of their debts back by fishing. Atlantic white cod would have been the fish of choice, though they would have also had access to other fish like runs Atlantic salmon. Here’s a linguini with salmon cream sauce recipe that makes use of the leftover, extra meat after filleting a fish.

Bring a large stock pot with salted water to a boil over high heat and cook your pasta according to the directions on the package. Reserve one cup of the pasta water before draining. Drain the noodles and set aside in a colander until ready to use.

In a large pan, melt the butter over medium heat, add the shallots and garlic, and cook until soft (about 2 minutes). Season with a pinch of salt, and black pepper to taste. Add the wine and cook until almost all the wine is evaporated. Add the heavy cream and the parmesan and stir together, cooking until the cream thickens up a bit (1-2 minutes). Add the pasta and toss with the cream sauce. If the sauce is too thick, add some of the pasta water until you get a creamy sauce. Toss in the parsley, and serve topped with grated parmesan. This will make six healthy servings.

Deer meat was likely the centerpiece of the first thanksgiving. After all, the Wampanoag brought five deer with them to the feast. Simple but effective, here’s the best way to apply heat to a backstrap and achieve perfection. And, just in case you have five deer on hand and a village to feed, here’s a guide on how to cook every scrap of meat on them.

So where did this turkey thing come from anyway? The one other written account from the autumn of 1621 does mention that the pilgrims had turkey, although nobody is certain that it was eaten at the feast. The second account from William Bradford states:

“And besides waterfowl there was great store of wild turkeys, of which they took many, besides venison, etc.”

Long after Bradford’s death, his journal was found and reprinted in the 1850s, and for some reason, people really liked the part about turkey. During that time, Sarah Josepha Hale, the editor of a magazine called Godey’s Lady’s Book, promoted the turkey as a centerpiece of the table. Hale was also a strong voice behind Thanksgiving Day becoming a national holiday. She wrote letters and even petitioned a few presidents.

Finally, in 1863, Abraham Lincoln declared the day a national holiday, and turkey has been the star of the show ever since. Whether wild turkey was eaten during the first Thanksgiving or not, it’s still delicious. If you have a left-over gobbler from the spring, or one you’ve shot this fall, this wild take on a classic Thanksgiving turkey recipe is sure to get some attention at your table.

• 2 gallons water • 2 oranges • 2 lemons • 1 onion, cut into 8 pieces • 1 cup brown sugar • 1 cup Kosher salt • Couple sprigs of fresh thyme or rosemary

Make brining mixture, mixing all ingredients. Squeeze the oranges and lemons into the mixture and toss in the rinds too. Soak turkey in a cooler with ice and the brining mixture overnight. If you need more brine, use ½ cup salt and ½ cup brown sugar for every gallon of water. Use additional fruit as desired.

I lightly stuff the turkey with a couple celery stalks, onion pieces and a couple carrots, along with a half lemon and half orange from the brine mixture.

1. Place the turkey breast side up on a rack in a shallow roasting pan. Do not add water.

2. Before placing the turkey in the oven, you may want to brush it with cooking oil, melted butter or margarine, although it’s not necessary.

3. Cover the turkey with a loose tent of heavy-duty aluminum foil to prevent over browning, allow for maximum heat circulation and keep the turkey moist. To make a tent, tear off a sheet of foil 5 to 10 inches longer than the turkey. Crease the foil crosswise through the center and place over the turkey, crimping loosely onto the sides of the pan to hold it in place.

5. To brown the turkey, remove the foil tent 20 to 30 minutes before roasting is finished, and continue cooking until the meat thermometer reaches 185 F.

The following times are based on an oven preheated to 325 F. Use shorter cooking times for wild turkey so it doesn’t dry out.

#8211. The Best Binoculars of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more

Every hunter needs a good binocular. But not every hunter needs a great one, and the difference between good and great seems to get slimmer every year. Having tested binoculars for going on a couple decades now, I’m perennially shocked by how good mid-priced models have become—to the point where the average hunter has to strain himself to see the difference between the very best and really good ones that cost half as much, or less. That’s great news for all of us.

But there is a difference between good and great. If you’re someone who’ll sit behind your glass for half a day trying tease antlers from a sea of sagebrush or count tines at 1,000 yards, you’ll want to know which ones are truly top-shelf. If you’re on a budget, however, or you hunt mostly mix-woods whitetails, for example, really good might be more than good enough for your needs. And a lot easier on your wallet.

The question is, which is which? I have spent many weeks over the past several years putting the top hunting binoculars through the wringer to find out. Several of the binoculars listed below are brand new for 2026; others debuted a year or more ago. All represent the latest full-size hunting models from each company. You can check out the “How We Test Binoculars” section below to see exactly how I evaluated each binocular. What I’ll say for now is that ours is one of the toughest tests out there. Why so rigorous? Well, to help you, of course. That is, to help you identify the absolute best binoculars, as well as the really good ones that might suit your hunting to a tee and save you a few bucks in the bargain. Here’s the lowdown.

In 2022, Zeiss introduced their remarkable SFL 10×40. The binocular immediately won this test’s Best Overall award and stayed at the top our list through 2025. Now, Zeiss is offering the SFL in three additional configurations, including an 8×50, 10×50, and 12×50. So, I decided to test the 10×50 to make sure that the SFL is as good as ever and to see what the 10×50 configuration brings to the party.

Obviously, I wasn’t disappointed, but let’s quickly review what made the original such a big deal when it came out. It’s rare to see something truly game-changing in this field. Binocular manufacturers can’t come out with a new caliber or make their product modular. But every once in a while, a company finds a new way to make the same old thing much better—and that is what Zeiss did with the SFL 10×40.

By using a sturdy-yet-ultralight frame and a groundbreaking design that places thinner lenses closer together, Zeiss delivered outstanding optical performance in a lighter, more compact package. The 10×40 weighs a featherlight 22.6 ounces and is still an absolute joy to hunt with.

The new 10×50 is significantly larger and heavier, but for a high-end 10×50, it a dream. (Yes, you can find cheap 10x50s that weigh less, but do you want a cheap binocular?) At 30.8 ounces, the SFL 10×50 weighs right about the same as several top-tier 10x42s on this list and about 5 ounces less than several popular high-end 10x50s, including one on this list.

Just like the original SFL 10×40, the new 10×50 scored extremely well in all of our test categories. Resolution and overall image quality were both near the top, coming in just a tick below the Swarovski NL Pure (see below). Build quality, ergonomics, and weather resistance were also at or near the top. And with its larger exit pupil, the SFL 10×50 excelled in low-light performance. I was surprised to see noticeable color shift in my testing, in which high contrast subjects appear to be fringed with yellow-green and/or purple bars of light. This shouldn’t be an issue in most hunting situations, but it is there. In the end, with its smooth focus wheel and big, bright image, Zeiss’s latest delivers 10×50 light-gathering performance in package that handles more like a good 10×42.

Personally, for most of my hunting, I’d still take the 22.6-ounce 10×40, which remains available and is as great as ever. But because the 10×50 is newer and, along with the other new configurations, gives you more options in an already outstanding binocular, it get’s my 2026 Best Overall award. And as was the case with for the 10x40s, part of the reason is value. I know, $1,799 is hardly chump change for a binocular. But for a binocular this good, it is actually kind of a bargain. Ounce-for-ounce and dollar-for-dollar, the Zeiss SFL 10×50 (or the 10×40 if you prefer) is as good as it gets in 2026.

Perfect scores in resolution and image quality

It’s true that the gap between good and great binoculars is closing. But a few still stand totally apart. The Swarovski NL Pure was the only binocular in this test to notch perfect scores in resolution and image quality, but it’s not enough to say that its optical performance is the best or even perfect. It’s more like a revelation. You look through this binocular and say “Wow!”—repeatedly.

I took the NL Pure 10×42 on an elk and deer hunt in Montana recently. At one point, we were glassing a bedded whitetail buck from long ways off, trying to figure out if he was worth a stalk. I was looking through the NL Pure and a buddy was looking through another $1,000-plus premium binocular. Studying the deer, I said, “He’s got decent mass but isn’t super tall or wide. He might go 130.” My buddy asked how I’d gotten all that from so far away. I handed him the NL Pure, he looked through them, and he said “Holy sh*t!” Then he studied the buck for minute and said, “Yup. Maybe 125.”

That’s what next-level resolution does for you, and it makes a real difference in the field. But world-class glass like this offers more than just stunning detail; it immerses you in the image. An optics professor I used to test binoculars with calls this “feeling of immersion.” With the NL Pure’s huge field of view and field-flattening lenses, you get the sense that you’ve stepped into the picture and that everything there is brilliant and vivid and free of the little imperfections that otherwise distract you from the experience.

The NL Pure’s innovative hour-glass, open-bridge design not only saves weight but balances perfectly in the hand, making it easy to stabilize the binocular on long glassing sessions, and an available forehead rest adds to the comfort. The focus wheel is large, precise, and silky. The diopter and eyecup adjustments are positive and exact.

All of that said, the NL Pure is not flawless. To my surprise, it pretty much bombed the weather-resistance test. After the submersion portion, the image was useable but not especially clear, and it was close to unusable coming out of the deep freeze. Again, our test is tougher than what most hunters will face in the outdoors, but still, in an apples-to-apples comparison, only one binoculars on this list did worse.

That, however—and the price (oof!)—are the NL Pure’s only flaws. In every other way, this binocular is spectacular. Give it a little extra protection in the weather, and it will show you things other hunters will never see.

The Monarch M7 is not quite Nikon’s top-end binocular. (That would be the Monarch HG, which has been the company’s flagship model for 10 years now and remains a very good binocular at a good price.) The Monarch M7 is, however, the latest in Nikon’s popular and rugged Monarch line, and it brings some of the same qualities—and value—as the HGs.

Like so many binos with the Monarch name, the M7 exudes toughness; you put it in your hands and know instantly that you can hunt hard with the thing, thanks to its obvious build quality and thick rubber armoring. What you can’t tell instantly but was born out in the weather-resistance testing is that the optics themselves are just as rugged and reliable. Only one binocular did better in our brutal test, and only by half a point—and that binocular (the Zeiss above) costs more than three times as much.

The M7’s ED glass delivered solid optical performance. Naturally, resolution and image quality was a step below the top-end glass, with a bit of tunneling, color shift, and blurring at the edges. Low-light performance was only O.K., but still not way off that of binoculars costing twice as much or more. The M7 got a nearly perfect score for handling; it fits nicely in your hands and feel good there, too, with it’s tacky rubber coating. The locking diopter is just what it should be, and although it’s a small thing, the objective lens caps, in terms of actually staying on the binocular, are as good as any and better than most. Where the M7 really shines, though, is value. For right around $500, you get a lightweight, compact full-size binocular that will hunt as hard as you do and deliver solid optical performance all the while. You can’t ask for much more than that.

If you had $1,000 to spend on a binocular—that is, you wanted something really good but didn’t want to shell out for the absolute best—here’s what I’d tell you: “Find another $150 and get the Meopta MeaPro Air.” Or, “Wait for this one to go on sale and snap it up.” Had I scored the test categories with letter grades, this binocular would have averaged an A-minus across the board, ranging from quite good to very good in every category and not at all bad in any.

Where the MeaPro Air did stand out was in image quality, low-light performance, and weather-resistance. Meopta’s Czech glass is just a tiny step below the very best, delivering fine clarity, true, vibrant colors, and a great feeling of immersion, thanks in part to a generous field of view. It sailed through the weather-resistance test, delivering a quite-good image after submersion and a perfectly useful image after being frozen. The rubber-reinforced magnesium body is reasonably lightweight but tough, and the open-bridge design feels good in the hand. The focus wheel on my test model was a tad stiff and the non-locking diopter possibly just loose enough to bump out of whack on occasion—but this is nit picking. What you have here is a binocular that is just shy of the very best, at a well-shy-of-the-very-best price.

With this upgraded UHD model, Vortex’s premium Razor goes from “High Definition” to “Ultra High Definition”—a distinction that doesn’t always mean much, as these are marketing terms, but in this case boils down to one hell of a good binocular that’s even better than the last iteration. Resolution is quite good, but it’s the image quality and low-light performance that really grab you. The Razor’s clarity, feeling of immersion (the sense that you are stepping into the picture), and lack of visual artifact gave even the top-scoring Swaro a run for its money in the optical categories. This combined with the comparatively large exit pupil also helped the Razor notch the best low-light score in the test.

Build quality and ergonomics are also first-rate. The focus wheel is smooth and precise, and the locking diopter adjustment is about perfect. The only categories where the Razor fell down a bit were handling and value. So, let’s take them one at a time. Yes, the Razor is noticeably larger and heavier than most models here. But with few exceptions (like the Zeiss above), the very best binoculars run on the heavy side, and, of course, the larger objective lenses contribute to the low-light performance. So, it’s a trade-off. If you want to see right up to the very edge of darkness, the extra size and weight may well be worth it to you. As for value, the MSRP price of $2,749 sure isn’t pocket change, but I’ve seen this binocular on sale for under $2K, which is perfectly fair for a true premium binocular that’s right there with the very best.

The B.6, Maven’s newest full-size hunting binocular, is essentially their flagship B1.2 souped up with larger objective lenses and a larger Schmidt-Pechan prism for better low-light performance. But here’s the real kicker: They managed to make these upgrades while adding only 3.9 ounces to the overall package. This means that the B.6 10×50 is even lighter (by an ounce) than the wonderfully lightweight Best-Overall-winning Zeiss SFL 10×50 above.

Overall optical performance was half a step down from the other 10x50s in this test, but so is the price (in fact, more like a step and a half in the case of the Vortex Razor). Compared to the other roughly $1,000 binoculars in this test, resolution, feeling of immersion, and edge-to-edge clarity were right on par and solidly in the Very Good category. There was some noticeable color shift, but that’s not uncommon and shouldn’t be an issue in most hunting situations.

Where the B.6 stood out was in low-light performance, ergonomics and handling, and weather-resistance. Maven optics tend to be popular with western mountain hunters where the weather can get brutal, and the B.6s performance in my very tough weather-resistance test shows why. They delivered anywhere between a very good image to a perfectly useful image in every phase of the test. The knurled-aluminum finish on the focus wheel (which was smooth and precise) and diopter (which has the perfect tension) are nice touches on binocular that doesn’t just look sharp but is also built very tough.

Bottom line: If your budget tops out at $1,200 and your main priorities are to have a reasonably lightweight binocular that lets you resolve detail at the very edges of dawn and dusk, then the B.6 should be perfect for you.

GPO stands for German Precision Optics, which references the fact that their scopes and binoculars are designed and engineered at the company headquarters in Germany, while the glass is sourced and the products manufactured primarily in Japan. According to the company, this arrangement has allowed them to offer European-like quality at a better price. The Passion HD has been their flagship binocular for some time and has always done well in our tests, especially in terms of optical performance.

Nothing has changed there. Only three binoculars on this list scored better than the GPO for resolution, and the same is true for image quality. Low-light performance was solid, if not quite great, and if you need a binocular that can deliver a clear image under virtually any conditions, the Passion HD is one, notching a near-perfect score in the weather-resistance test. It delivered a comparatively clear image after being submersed in water and a perfectly usable image coming out of the deep freeze.

When I originally tested this binocular, I had some trouble with the locking diopter built into the focus wheel. But GPO sent me another, saying that the problem had been fixed. And in fact it was. The diopter on the newer example worked perfectly. The only knock I have on the Passion HD is that I don’t love its feel in the hand; I find the coating a little hard and slick. But that’s a small point, and you may like it just fine. Most important, the Passion HD’s optical performance fits its price tag, and you can find it for closer to $900 if you poke around.

This is a very good binocular for $800. If the Nikon wasn’t so much less, this would have gotten the Best Value award. Tract Optics has made a name for itself as a direct-to-consumer brand that offers solid quality for a better price, and their Toric binocular has been a fine example of this for years—and remains so. It’s latest iteration, the UHD Toric has been upgraded with Schott HT extra-low dispersion glass, and the result is a lightweight, compact, full-size binocular that’s built very tough and feels good in the hand, with excellent rubber armoring and nice all-around ergonomics—all at a very fair price.

What about the optics? Resolution and low-light performance was right there with the $1,000 models and even a bit better than some. Image quality is quite good, too, with a bright, inviting picture. There is a bit of blurring at the edges of the image and a slight tunneling effect, but both are minor. The Toric aced my very tough weather-resistance test, has an impressively smooth focus wheel, and a good, locking diopter. All in all, this $800 binocular holds its own optically with models costing a couple hundred bucks more, and it feels a little better in the hand and is sharper looking than several, too.

Leupold’s top-end binocular, the BX-5 Santiam HD has a similar quality to the Nikon Monarch M7 in that you pick it up and you know it’ll take a beating—that you can hunt hard with it and not worry. This one, though, comes in a more refined package. The build quality, fit and finish, and ergonomics of the Santiam are first rate. The knurled rubber armoring and open-bridge design combined with the compact size and light weight make for a binocular that feels great in the hand.

There’s a bit of a trade off in resolution, as this binocular scored a tick below others in its price range, partly due to some noticeable color shift. But it made up for it with solid scores in image quality and low-light performance and excellent scores in weather-resistance and handling. There was some edge blurring and a bit of tunneling, but the image is bright and vibrant. The focus wheel is about perfect, as is the tension on the non-locking diopter. My general feeling about the Santiam is that I would like it a lot if it cost just a little less. And low and behold, it kind of does. While the MSRP is $1,099, you can find it for closer to $900 if you poke around.

For decades, Field & Stream has been putting hunting glass through rigorous testing to help readers separate the great from the very good and the good from the garbage—and we’re not afraid to tell you which is which. You wont find a tougher, more thorough, or more honest optics test. Binocular manufacturers, to their credit, have always been on board to submit their products for evaluation.

Because binocular manufacturers do not unveil new products every year, I invited optics companies to send their best, most-recent full-size binocular in for testing. Upon their arrival, I checked each model to make sure they met advertised specs, and then I spent weeks on the range and in the field running them through a long list of tests and evaluations to determine how they all stack up.

I evaluated each binocular for the following eight categories:

Resolution: I set up a 1951 USAF Resolution Test Chart and a color-artifact test at 50 yards and recorded values for each binocular corresponding to detail resolved and color shift perceived.

Image Quality: In a variety of landscapes and lighting situations, I evaluated each binocular’s image for clarity, feeling of immersion, and visual artifacts, including stray light and apparent field curvature (or blurring at the edges).

Low-Light Performance: This category aggregated exit pupil and low-light resolution, using a 1951 USAF Resolution Test Chart set up in the dark and lit only by a far-way flood light. (Why not at dawn and dusk? Because fading or growing light makes it impossible to compare each on a level playing field.)

Build Quality and Ergonomics: I judged overall feel in the hand, as well as the quality, feel, and functionality of the focus wheel, eyepieces, diopter adjustment, and lens covers.

Weather Resistance: I submersed each binocular in a creek next to my house for a half hour, then took them out and scored them for image quality and resolution. Then I put them in a chest freezer for a half hour and rated them on image, resolution, and functionality immediately after and again a half-hour after coming out of the deep freeze.

Handling: All else being equal, the lighter and more compact a binocular, the better, which is why this category is a straight reflection of each test model’s size and weight.

I scored each binocular on a 1 to 10 scale for all the categories above and then double the key ones or resolution (because seeing fine detail, like antler points, at distance is a big deal to most hunters), image quality (because it can make extended viewing so much more comfortable and enjoyable), and weather-resistance (because we need our binos to work no matter what), for a total possible score of 100 points.

For more than 125 years, Field & Stream has been providing readers with honest and authentic coverage of outdoor gear. Our writers and editors eat, sleep, and breathe the outdoors, and that passion comes through in our product reviews. You can count on F&S to keep you up to date on the best new gear. And when we write about a product—whether it’s a bass lure or a backpack—we cover the good and the bad, so you know exactly what to expect before you decide to make a purchase.

Dave Hurteau took the position of assistant editor at Field & Stream in 1994, and has been with the brand ever since. His first job was to work on F&S’s 100th anniversary issue, and in 2020, he helped spearhead the 125th. In that span, he’s worked with many of the magazine’s greats, from Gene Hill and Bob Brister to Bill Heavey, and David E. Petzal. Highlights Education Hurteau graduated from the University of Rochester with degrees in English and philosophy, the latter of which helped him to rationalize the days spent hunting and fishing in western New York when he should have been in class. Experience After graduating college, Hurteau launched a regional hunting and fishing magazine from an apartment in Ithaca, New York, and soon parlayed that into the job at Field & Stream. He’s had no less than eight titles with F&S, from gear editor to contributing writer and, now, executive editor. He’s been nominated for a National Magazine Award as a writer and was part of an F&S editorial team to win two National Magazine Awards for General Excellence—the highest honor in magazine journalism. Hurteau oversees much of the brand’s hunting, gear, and general outdoors coverage. An serious hunter and angler himself, he is co-author of The Total Deer Hunter Manual and the The Total Bowhunting Manual. #8208. 11 Deals at Evo’s Black Friday Sale That Seem Too Good to be True

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

(Photo: Courtesy of Head, Yardsale, Kari Traa, Evo, Arc'teryx, and Oyuki)

Savvy shoppers know Black Friday is the Super Bowl of savings. These days, it’s more like Black Friday Week, which gives us even more time to browse the best deals.

For skiers, there’s no better time to refresh your gear closet than November, when you start taking stock of what you own and what you need for the season. The good news is that Evo is a one-stop shop for everything from hard goods to travel bags, and the deals are plentiful. Keep reading to see what the SKI team is recommending from Evo’s big Black Friday sale.

We’ll admit it’s not the sexiest gift on anyone’s list, but Evo’s Roller Ski Bag is on sale, and it’s a no-brainer for ski travelers who want to bring their own skis and ensure they arrive safely at their destination. The bag has wheels, which is essential for hauling skis through airports and parking lots. It also holds up to two pairs of skis, poles, boots, outerwear, and accessories, all in padded, durable compartments. Internal straps keep everything in place, and the bag folds up for compact storage between trips. —Samantha Berman

I’ve long appreciated the Arc’teryx Sentinel for its clean, understated design and thoughtful features. It’s a serious technical shell without a lot of unnecessary bells and whistles, and the weather protection is hard to beat.

What I especially like is the longer, freeride-inspired silhouette, which provides plenty of coverage over my hips and works well with bibs. The fit feels streamlined without being restrictive, and I can comfortably wear a lightweight puffy underneath on colder days. When the weather turns, the three-layer GORE-TEX construction and helmet-compatible StormHood help seal out wind and snow.

The latest Sentinel has been updated with a tougher 100-denier face fabric, a refined fit, larger hand pockets, and a new chest pocket. It’s also designed for moving between the resort and backcountry, which is exactly the kind of versatility I look for in a shell.

The fabric is on the stiffer side, especially when new, and takes a little time to break in. But it isn’t excessively loud or crunchy, and I appreciate that rugged feel in a jacket designed for years of hard use. The Sentinel is a significant investment, so finding one on sale makes it a lot more appealing. —Sierra Shafer

I’m a big fan of getting dressed for skiing in the lodge instead of the parking lot, so I’m usually hauling my skis, boots, and assorted gear from the car. The Yardsale Day Bag makes that whole process a lot easier.

At 30 liters, it’s roomy enough to fit everything I need without becoming a bottomless black hole. The magnetic closures, internal divider, dedicated pockets, and key ring help keep smaller items organized, while the cinch closure makes it easy to throw in bulkier gear without worrying about things falling out. There’s even a padded laptop sleeve for days when I’m working from the mountain and hoping to sneak in a few lunch laps.

One of my favorite details is the suitcase sleeve, which lets me slide the bag securely over my rolling carry-on when I travel. No more tote bag constantly slipping off my shoulder or luggage at the airport.

It’s also plenty durable. I’ve shoved it under countless lodge tables, dragged it around on trips, and even spilled what appears to have been an entire glass of red wine inside it. Most of the evidence came out in the wash, and I still reach for this bag constantly. —SS

I’m firmly in the mittens-over-gloves camp. They’re warmer, more comfortable, and I’ve been skiing in Oyuki mittens for years. I’ve worn every pair I’ve owned until the insulation eventually packed out, usually after four or five seasons of heavy use. That kind of longevity has made me a loyal fan.

The Sencho GORE-TEX mittens combine waterproof protection with warm PrimaLoft insulation and a soft wool lining. What I especially like about OYUKI mittens is how supple and comfortable they feel, without the excessive bulk that can make some mittens frustrating to wear. I can still manage poles, zippers, and most of the little tasks that come up throughout a ski day without constantly taking them off.

The wrist coverage helps eliminate that annoying gap between your mittens and jacket sleeves, while the leashes mean I can pull them off on the chairlift without worrying about losing one.

I also love the brand’s Japanese roots. Oyuki means “big snow,” and the kanji in its logo translates to “smash pow.” How can you not love that? —SS

When I reach for an insulated jacket on a resort ski day, odds are high it’s the Halfdays Georgie puffer. It’s one of the brand’s original styles, and it’s a classic for a reason. The 550-fill body is warm without being bulky, and the 15,000mm waterproof rating keeps you dry all day on a powder day. My favorite features are the pockets, which were clearly designed by people who ski: they’re intuitively placed and even come with a goggle wipe and a phone leash. The snap-removable hood fits over practically every helmet, too. The dark green colorway is currently on sale, and it just so happens to be on my wishlist.

Evo is also offering a bundle deal for the Georgie Puffer and Alessandra Pants for $644 (down from $920) —Jamie Aranoff

The Hydra Thermagraph delivers impressive performance and style for the price, making it one of the better values in women’s ski outerwear—especially at its Black Friday discount. It pairs a waterproof, breathable 20K infiDRY shell with Thermagraph body-mapped insulation that puts warmth where you need it rather than throughout. Add in features including underarm vents, a helmet-compatible hood, a powder skirt, and generous pockets—including a dedicated phone heater pocket—and you’ve got a jacket that can handle everything from frigid chairlift rides to deep powder days. —SB

The Stio Pinion Down Hooded Jacket is one of those versatile layers that earns its keep well beyond ski season. Its lightweight, packable design and water-resistant 800-fill HyperDRY down make it an excellent layer under a shell, adding warmth without unnecessary bulk. The clean, casual styling also makes it a solid everyday grab for walking the dog, running errands, or grabbing après beers. It’s a worthwhile Black Friday upgrade for the minimalist on your list who doesn’t like to waste closet space. —SB

I first fell for the Head Kore 94 at SKI Test, and it has quickly become one of my favorites. It carried me through Utah’s unusually warm winter, when I needed a ski that wasn’t afraid of a little ice. On the few powder days we did get, it stayed afloat better than expected, and never felt like it was sinking. It’s a jack of all trades, which is exactly what I want in a daily driver. The 2027 model is out now, but there’s not a huge change from 2026, so snagging these for under $400 is a win. —JA

The Cotopaxi Tasra 16L Backpack hits the sweet spot as a ski-day pack: compact enough to stay out of your way on the lift, but roomy enough to carry the essentials, from an extra layer and snacks to water, sunscreen, and other necessities. Its 16-liter capacity keeps you from overstuffing it, while multiple pockets, dual water-bottle sleeves, and a durable recycled-polyester construction make it a practical choice. —SB

Kari Traa makes base layers for the girls who shred. I absolutely love my sets from this brand, founded by an Olympian, and I find that the capri pants never slip down, which is seriously important when it comes to successful layering. These 100-percent merino wool pieces will keep you warm all day, and when you start to sweat, they’ll keep you dry, too. Mix and match patterns for a fun base layer that’ll last for many seasons to come. —JA

I’ve skied almost exclusively in Le Bent socks for years, and the Compression Zero Cushion is a favorite. It took me a while to come around to compression socks, but now I appreciate the supportive fit, especially on long days in ski boots.

I prefer a really thin ski sock because I like being able to feel my boot, and Le Bent’s blend of merino wool and bamboo-derived rayon does an excellent job managing moisture. There’s a misconception that thicker socks are always warmer, but a thin, moisture-wicking sock helps keep your feet dry, which goes a long way toward keeping them warm. And in a snug ski boot, extra bulk can compromise fit and circulation.

The compression is noticeable without feeling restrictive, and the socks stay put all day. No sliding, no bunching, no annoying wrinkles inside my boots, even when I’m touring and moving around a lot more than I would on a resort day.

I also appreciate the height. I have long legs, and these come up high enough to meet my three-quarter-length base layers without leaving an uncomfortable gap of bare skin. They may not technically be on sale at evo this Black Friday, but I’m still taking the reminder to repurchase before ski season starts in earnest.—SS

#8207. Escape Winter With These 6 Underrated Desert Trail Runs

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

In his research for his upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” Andy Cochrane ran hundreds of trails across the U.S. These are his six favorites across the Southwest that come into season when most of the country is hibernating.

With all due respect to Presidential Traverse, Teton Crest, and Wonderland, the most sought-after one-day trail running route in the U.S. is the Grand Canyon Rim-to-Rim-to-Rim. Every spring and fall runners flock to Arizona to test their luck on this double lap of the big ditch, despite the National Park Service strongly advising against it. (Signs around the Grand Canyon warn of heat illness, elevation, and difficult evacs.)

Some have called R2R2R an obsession—while I’m not sure I would personally go that far, I do see the argument. I’ve run the route three times and each trip I find myself more enamored than the last. On my last visit in 2023, a peak autumn weekend with nearly perfect temps and all the water facets still running (the NPS shuts some of them down seasonally), I saw hundreds of runners attempting R2R2R. That’s a tiny fraction of the four and a half million people who visit the park each year, but very busy for a trail run.

However, that was before the closures. The North Rim of the Grand Canyon was shuttered for most of the 2025 season due to the Dragon Bravo Fire, which burned 149,000 acres and 118 buildings. Then, on August 29th, 2026, a flash flood struck Phantom Ranch at the bottom of the Grand Canyon, killing three and forcing 82 others to be evacuated by helicopter. Trail damage was widespread, taking out footbridges and much of the park’s water line. The North Kaibab Trail, parts of the Bright Angel and South Kaibab trails, and sections of the River Trail remain closed with no set date for reopening.

It’s getting colder and darker across most of the country. That means one thing: It’s desert season. In lieu of a double dip into the Grand Canyon—and to open your mind to the endless possibilities elsewhere—I’ve compiled a list of my six favorite trails across the American Southwest. All of them are in my upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” (which you can pre-order now!). They cover six different states and four unique desert ecosystems, so there is plenty of variety to choose from.

Unlike the rocky singletrack of the Northeast, the forested trails of the upper Midwest, or the alpine ridges of the West, running across the Southwest desert is a singular experience. Limited shade, even less water, and direct solar radiation create obvious hydration challenges. The temperature swings dramatically from near freezing overnight to scorching heat midday. The trails themselves are a mix of surfaces, from soft sand to loose scree to firm slickrock, with many—including the ones listed below—being very remote.

Beyond the physical experience, running in arid environments carries a different emotion, too. I often find myself in a quiet and contemplative mental space, passing by ancient saguaros, joshua trees, and prickly pears while trying to stay alert for subtle movements of rattlesnakes, lizards, and coyotes. Running in the desert is, simultaneously, the antidote to life’s complexity and a plague of endless possibility.

There are four distinct desert ecosystems in the U.S. The northernmost is the Great Basin, which covers most of Nevada and parts of neighboring states, making it the largest desert in the country. With frigid winters, it’s filled with sagebrush instead of cacti. Just south is the Mojave, the smallest of the four, which is home to Death Valley and Joshua Tree. Further south is the Sonoran, the “green desert,” with large saguaros and rainfall in both summer and winter. Last, the Chihuahuan, covers West Texas and southern New Mexico, and is known for succulents like Agave, Yucca, and Creosote.

Hidden in one of North America’s most remote national parks, Big Bend, the Outer Mountain Loop is a 32-mile circuit featuring a stark ecological contrast between the Chihuahuan Desert and the high-alpine Chisos Mountains. Beginning and ending in the Chisos Basin, a sky-island that’s home to rare species like the Colima Warbler, the trail plunges down stone steps and rolls across the sun-scorched flats of the Dodson Trail before making a grueling 3,000-foot final ascent up Blue Creek Canyon. Early Spanish explorers called this isolated region El Despoblado.

Why I love it: Getting to experience both sky islands and the solitude of the Chihuahuan desert.

Spanning 39 miles from the edge of the Navajo Nation to the Grand Canyon’s South Rim, the Little to Big Colorado route is the less conventional way to explore one of the country’s most popular national parks. Tracing the historic Hopi salt journeys, the route plunges down Bekihatso Wash, follows the Little Colorado to its confluence with the Colorado River, passes sacred sites, scrambles obstacles like the Papago Wall, and passes by billion-year-old rock. With a 4,700-foot grind up the New Hance Trail at the end, it’s just as challenging and rewarding as rim-to-rim-to-rim.

Why I love it: It’s so close to the most famous one day trail route in the country, but still unheard of.

Crossing the national park from east to west, this 37-mile rolling route passes two distinct deserts—the higher Mojave and the lower Sonora—as you wander by long shadows of Yucca brevifolia (Joshua trees) and massive, weathered granite batholiths. Championed by the activist Minerva Hamilton Hoyt after decades of cattle grazing and mining exploitation, this sandy sanctuary strips away the crowds, offering sheer solitude as runners cross ancient mountain passes, gaze down at the dark expanse of the Salton Sea, and experience a desert communion.

Why I love it: it’s the one place in America that feels straight out of a Dr. Seuss book.

One of the most remote routes we considered for the book, this 64-mile trek traces the ridgeline of the Toiyabe Range. Like Outer Mountain, this area is a sky island, a rare ecosystem in which the valley below is a scorching hot desert, but the trail itself is a lush forest of aspen and bristlecone pines, some 3,000 years old. Despite being Nevada’s longest named trail, Toiyabe is off-trail in nature, with significant routefinding and some sections of unrunnable terrain.

Why I love it: Remote and rugged, it’s a good test of navigation and alpine movement of all sorts.

Perched above Albuquerque, this 26-mile trail follows a limestone ridge along the backbone of the Sandia Mountains, with 360-degree views of the Rio Grande Valley below. Sandia is Spanish for watermelon, named after the ridge’s unique sunset alpenglow that turns the cliffs deep pink, with green conifers on top representing the rind. The trail features wildflowers, ponderosas, spruce, and white fir, and can be accessed via an aerial tramway, providing easy access without sacrificing its rugged, aesthetic appeal.

Why I love it: Quick and easy access paired with absolutely beautiful sunsets.

Winding through one of Southern Utah’s most distinctive landscapes, the 30-mile Bryce Canyon Traverse links the heavily trafficked northern amphitheater where thousands of hoodoos, rock fins, and natural arches create a natural maze with the primitive Under the Rim Trail to the south. Crossing a geological marvel shaped by erosion and freeze-thaw cycles over millions of years, the traverse is the best way to see it all. Heading southbound allows runners to catch sunrise over the spires before descending into remote backcountry, which is the direction we recommend.

Why I love it: There’s no place in the world with the same density or volume of hoodoos.

Desert running presents many challenges that the Mafate X can handle. Deserts are often oven-hot, so having a woven, high-airflow upper is ideal. They are rocky and filled with pokey things, so having a taller stack with soft PEBA foam is a bonus. They are loose, so having Vibram lugs adds a level of stability and confidence. And, with uneven ground, a wide base makes your feet feel much more planted, too.

On long, sweaty days, sunscreen only goes so far. I take extra precaution and wear a Tahoe sun hoody, which delivers UPF 50+ protection against harsh UV rays, paired with a light polyester-spandex knit that wicks sweat off my skin and dries quickly. And, integrated thumbholes and a fitted hood keep my hands and neck completely covered without restricting movement.

For most desert runs I recommend stashing water the day before, but if you aren’t able to, having an extra large running pack is key. Kiprun’s 10L has room for a bladder in the back and two flasks up front, which is ideal for long desert stretches. The harness keeps the pack secure and large front pockets make it easy to access your phone, electrolytes, snacks, or sunscreen on the go.

My favorite drink mix, Fuel combines essential electrolytes like sodium, potassium, and magnesium to replace minerals lost in heavy sweat. It tastes good, prevents cramps, and the added zinc supports fluid retention in hot conditions. Using a low-GI carb from beet sugar, it also provides steady energy without blood sugar spikes or crashes, which is great for longer days.

#8205. A Climber We Lost: Jun Kyu Kim

On August 21, 2026, Jun Kyu Kim was scrambling on the approach to a climb in Eldorado Canyon, when he fell. Even though he was wearing a helmet, he suffered a fatal head injury. The tragedy shook the Denver climbing community he had been a part of. Jun touched so many lives, whether through Cruxing in Color, of which he was an early supporter, or at the crag, where he was known to offer kind advice and encouraging words. He leaves behind his loving family, his girlfriend, and so many friends whose lives were made better by his generosity and kindness.

Born on April 3, 1981, Jun was raised by his loving parents Hyoun Sook Kim and Ho Young Kim, and grew up in Chicago with his two sisters. Throughout his life, Jun was known for his adventurous spirit and zest for exploration. He discovered his love for the outdoors—where he found peace and joy—at an early age during a National Outdoor Leadership School trip to Alaska. It was during high school that he was introduced to rock climbing, which quickly became his true passion.

Jun once said that climbing was the thing he lived for. In the climbing community, he was known for his trademark red hat, dirtbag clothes, love for donuts, and his patented naps. He could sleep anytime and anywhere, then upon waking, send his project. After completing a route, he’d often be out like a light. Ever a favorite climbing partner, he exuded confidence, patience, and calm under pressure. And he settled people’s nerves, allowing them to achieve ever harder things. When friends would get down on themselves about their climbing, he was always the first to remind them to not take climbing so seriously, to have fun, and to give themselves grace on high gravity days.

I spoke with Jun’s girlfriend, Sz-min Harley, and his best friend, Shawnee, to learn more about what Jun meant to the people he climbed with. Many people saw him as a mentor. He would frequently take less experienced climbers under his wing. But he also was famous for sandbagging. If you accepted his suggestion, you knew you could be in for a far more difficult adventure than you had counted on. But Jun’s encouraging words, infectious laughter, and love for fun would make it all worth the story in the end. Shawnee says that the first time they climbed together was in El Salto, where he had Shawnee try his warm-up. She could barely get halfway up before she had to come down. Jun refused to tell Shawnee the grade, but she later found out it was a 5.12b.

Jun was also known for his love of cooking, something that he learned from his mom at a young age. He continued to cook with her until the end. For Jun, food was a love language. He liked few things better than bringing people together around a meal, whether in the kitchen or around a campfire. The first time he came to visit Shawnee, he drove six hours and showed up with a cooler full of homemade Korean dishes for her to try. Once, he cooked dinner for the 20 people who had signed up for his friends’ newly launched Beyond Jamming crack climbing clinic in Indian Creek. The entire crew came back from a full day of climbing, tired and hungry, to a grinning Jun. He had made homemade tacos for everyone, complete with vegetarian, gluten-free, and lactose-free options.

That was Jun—a man with an unbelievably big heart who was always looking for a way to help and who showed up every day for his friends. He was the kind of friend who would always be there for you, whether you needed a belay on a project or a partner willing to head out to that route tucked away in a far corner of the desert. Never letting the friendship fade, Jun was known for checking in on the people he loved, making sure you knew that he was thinking of you. He would help fix your van, make you chicken soup when you were sick, and send you a card just to say he was glad you existed. Not only did Jun give love from the bottom of his heart, but he did it without expecting anything in return.

Jun’s friend Adien shared something that has stuck with me: “Jun was a rare, selfless climber. He would go to the crag for himself, but he would go for you.”

Climbing took Jun all over the world—Thailand, Greece, Columbia, Cuba, Chile, Mexico. But until the end, his favorite place was always Indian Creek. The first time he went, he and a friend only had four cams that they bumped up the routes, bearing miserably cold weather. Yet, the Creek still managed to claim his heart. Over the years, that love became even stronger and more special. Season after season, he made memories of hard sends, campfires, and laughter with his friends. For those who loved him, the Creek will never be the same.

Forty five years around the sun would never be enough, but Jun managed to fill those years with more life than most people do in twice as much time.

We miss you, Jun, and we will always carry you with us, keeping your spirit alive by choosing generosity, connection, and care.

#8203. The 7 Most Desperate Things I’ve Done in My Search for Ski Boots That Fit

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Seven states, two countries, three acupuncturists, and one orthopedist later, a skier with hard-to-fit feet found the bootfitter she needed. (Photo: Courtesy Abigail Barronian)

Overview: This first-person essay follows one skier’s years-long search for ski boots that fit, with bootfitters in seven states and two countries, a visit to an orthopedist, three acupuncturists, and a stranger’s garage. It’s a funny account of what hard-to-fit feet can drive a person to do, and a reminder that the right bootfitter can change everything.

In my quest for ski boots that fit, I’ve seen bootfitters in at least seven states and two countries. I’ve visited Evo and REI, small independent shops, local chains, and garages-turned-ski shops. I’ve consulted boot designers, brand reps, professional athletes, and gear reviewers; tried Intuitions, ZipFits, and custom footbeds. I’ve seen one orthopedic doctor, three acupuncturists, and two physical therapists. I’ve stayed up at night thinking about boots, and developed recurring stress dreams about them.

Last season, I was beginning to consider looping in a tarot reader or astrologer. Maybe I needed a psychotherapist, or a priest. Maybe I’d have to just quit skiing. And then, finally, I found my bootfitter. But not before resorting to some questionable behavior along the way. Here are seven desperate things I did in my search for a bootfitter who could solve my ski boot issues.

Every pair of ski boots I wore from ages two through 22 were hand-me-downs from my older brothers. Then I started working in the ski industry. While skiing around Big Sky during a media event, a kind man working for Nordica looked at my feet with a frown.

“What are those?” he asked. I was sliding around in some decade-old size 26.5 monstrosities. He shook his head and invited me to swing by the Nordica headquarters in New Hampshire. There, he measured my feet and sent me off with a pair of 25.5 Nordica Promachines.

Everything changed. Suddenly I was in an aggressive stance, my shins met real resistance, my power transfer improved dramatically. I got a taste of what a good boot can do, shortly before developing a wicked case of tendonitis in my ankles and shins.

After two seasons of excruciating, day-ending pain, I booked an appointment with an orthopedic foot and ankle specialist. I knew my boots were the culprit, and couldn’t be sure a doctor would understand the whole foot-encased-in-rigid-plastic thing. I lugged a giant bag with both my alpine and touring boots into the orthopedic practice and pulled them out for show-and-tell.

The physician kindly assured me he knew what ski boots were, and that I wasn’t dealing with any serious medical issues. I’d have to take my boots back where they belonged.

The owner of Santa Fe’s one dedicated ski shop sized me down yet again, into the stiffest 24.5 he had on hand—a 110 from Fischer. I felt like I was skiing in socks and a vise-grip at the same time, and I lost feeling in my feet on the first lap. Mercifully, he let me return them.

I’d hit the central problem: boots big enough to be comfortable gave me tendonitis, and boots small enough to prevent it gave me bunions and nerve pain. So I took my boots to Taos Bootdoctors, where a whole team of bootfitters worked patiently to expand the forefoot. I’d ski for a day or two and come back, over and over, looking for just a few more millimeters. I brought six-packs and did my best to be charming, and the lovely staff never made me feel less important than the tourists dropping thousands of dollars on gear. Still, I couldn’t finish a day without pain.

I soldiered through the season, eyeing an upcoming hut trip with dread. I could manage shorter tours, but a week of daylong missions posed some real problems. Once we were in the mountains, I knew no amount of bunion donuts and anti-inflammatories would save me. I had to instate boots-off breaks in the middle of eight-hour ski days, carefully pulling my socked feet out of jail and propping them up on a backpack in the snow while my friends took an extra lap. Sweet, stupid relief.

Finally, I heard a rumor about a man in Seattle working out of his garage who was willing to do unorthodox things to ski boots. He had a history of custom-fitting plug boots for ski racers, which seemed like a good sign. While visiting family in Washington, I brought him both pairs of boots.

He looked at my feet, listened patiently, and rattled off a comprehensive plan that involved several devices I’d never seen before. Overnight, he molded both pairs into a completely new shape. I never had to touch either boot again, and proceeded with great pleasure to ski 12-hour days in the backcountry and endless resort laps with happy feet. I had found him—the bootfitter I was looking for. Then, he retired.

When my touring boots started to go, I bought a replacement pair and nobody could make them fit. The experience began to take on mythic proportions. I felt like the princess with a pea beneath her many mattresses, or an ugly stepsister trying to cram her foot into a crystal slipper: all discomfort and wrong fit.

It seemed my trusty Tecnicas were the problem. I tried on every touring boot at ski shops in three states. I ordered over a dozen pairs online, obsessively double-checking return policies and momentarily racking up a very scary credit card bill. Eventually, I came crawling back to my old Tecnicas with no plan, two full seasons into the search.

I hesitated to say yes to ski trips, afraid I’d have to sit out ski days because of pain or busted gear. Eventually, it happened: I took my tired old touring boots to Rogers Pass in B.C. and, on day three, broke the upper cuff clean off the bottom section of the boot. Thankfully we were just a few hundred yards from the truck. I spent the entire day sitting at the trailhead.

In the meantime, my alpine boots had begun to warp. I found a replacement pair and was back at square one: home in New Mexico, with two pairs of ski boots that didn’t fit, rapidly dwindling patience, and no bootfitter.

I considered that this might be the end of the road for me as a skier. Then, I learned that one of the best skiers I know had been contemplating quitting the sport because of foot pain. He’d even gone so far as to teach himself to snowboard. But then he found exactly what I’d been looking for: yet another fit-obsessed industry veteran working out of his garage.

I visited another home workshop in western Washington and the bootfitter listened carefully as I explained the issue. Then, he overhauled both pairs of boots, tirelessly stretching the forefoots to give my feet room to breathe. They took on a completely new shape: generous and wide. I took both pairs out for a spin and sighed in relief.

There are a lot of great bootfitters out there. But for a freak like me, I’ve learned I need something of a mad scientist. If you’re plagued with bone spurs, high insteps, wide feet—there’s hope, I promise. With a little faith, a lot of persistence, and maybe something like divine intervention, I trust you’ll find the bootfitter you need. Let’s just hope they don’t retire.

#8201. The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level. Under our feet is a sharp slope of scree, a jumbled descent of rocks with patches of snow. The air is thin, and the vast Bolivian landscape surrounds us.

Directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain. El Alto, the chaotic concrete and red brick city that has grown to roughly 900,000 people, lies at the far edge of the plain at 13,000 feet of elevation, crammed against a canyon’s edge. About 1,500 feet below and connected by a series of cable cars, La Paz, Bolivia’s seat of government, sprawls.

Behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif. The nearly 20,000-foot summit towers above, its glaciated peak passing in and out of fast-moving clouds. About 45 miles to the northwest, Lake Titicaca—the central motif to Inca creation stories—shimmers on the horizon.

It’s here, on this high mountain of almost-bare rock cradled in the Andes, that Mendoza learned to ski.

Located roughly 20 miles north of La Paz, Chacaltaya was once the world’s highest-altitude ski resort. It began in the 1930s when Raúl Posnansky, an engineer and ski enthusiast, recognized the mountain’s potential, according to 2023 reporting by “Radio Ambulante.” Chacaltaya’s glacier, though relatively small in area at roughly 55 acres, was a solid tongue of ice descending the slope. Temperatures up high stayed low, and snow fell heavily and often during the wet season. The ice was there, had always been there, and would always be there, by all indications at the time.

Posnansky worked to materialize his skiing fantasy: He hired laborers to build an access road, haul materials, construct cabins, and install the first rope tow at Chacaltaya—powered by a truck engine housed in a cabin hanging over the base of the ski run.

Posnansky, along with other mountain athletes, founded the Club Andino Boliviano, a group of dedicated skiers and enthusiasts. To fund the growing ski scene, the club drew involvement from La Paz’s middle and upper classes, and Posnansky and the club persuaded Bolivia’s Congress to pass tax legislation dedicating 1% of the country’s hotel revenue to Bolivia’s Ski and Mountaineering Federation. This funding would help transform Chacaltaya from a passion project into the hub of Bolivian skiing—a hub that, while retaining its roughshod, backyard roots, would grow to host a national ski team, crowded weekend races, the first South American ski championships, and athletes who would represent the country at Winter Olympics.

When Mendoza was a young boy in El Alto, his family wasn’t connected to La Paz’s urban elite who would drive across the Altiplano to ski. Mendoza’s father, however, worked as the caretaker of Chacaltaya, often living for weeks at a time at the resort to maintain the facilities.

When he was 15, Mendoza accompanied his father to the mountain for the first time. He spent his first night at the base racked by altitude sickness.

“My dad gave me coca leaf tea,” he says. The next day, “the sun came out; I felt better. I got acclimated, and I learned to ski.”

Fifty years later, standing once again on the summit, Mendoza is transported back to the resort’s heyday.

“The rope would drop us off here,” he says. “And then …” He puts his hands on bent knees and waves them back and forth in a slalom. He raises his hands over his head and lets out a high yell, feeling the old rush of racing in the cold air.

Mendoza is in his 60s now. He has a harder time seeing, looking out through thick glasses, and his knees sometimes bother him.

Around us the glacier has completely vanished, leaving behind only a mountain of rock.

Infatuated with the world of snow and slopes, Mendoza learned to ski on gear borrowed from Club Andino. He worked long, physical days with his father, tasks ranging from construction and upkeep to manning the rope tow—including rebraiding the wire cable whenever it snapped, a job that left Mendoza with thin white scars across his fingers. From his father, he learned to manage the mountain, the two often sleeping in the lodge for weeks at a time.

Meanwhile, his love for skiing only deepened. Mendoza remembers Stanley Shepard, an American diplomat posted in Bolivia, who taught him advanced techniques and shared the joy of the mountain.

“Stan would drive up this road so fast,” he says as we drive the same route from the city to Chacaltaya some 50 years later. He smiles with the memory of the adrenaline rush.

Mendoza’s ski story exists in a split reality: In one, he is the caretaker’s son, surrounded by a country’s elites who lived near, but not next to, families like his. The socioeconomic divide paralleled the geography: La Paz’s wealthy neighborhoods in the valley, El Alto on the cold outcropping of the Altiplano above. Despite the divide, Mendoza was a vital member of the Chacaltaya scene; the members of Club Andino were his friends. The nights were full of music whenever others would sleep alongside him and his father at the refugio. The period is marked in Mendoza’s mind by shared meals in the cabin and shared runs on the mountain.

By the 1970s, with Chacaltaya entering its golden period, Mendoza was both employee and skier. He tells me he used to set up for the weekend slalom races—ones he’d often compete in as well. I ask about the slalom poles, curious about infrastructure. He tells me they were made nearby. “But the first times,” he says, “we used hollow canes, like cornstalks.”

In a 1976 article in Ski Magazine, American writer Jeff Frees described his visit to the ski hill. There were some two dozen weekly skiers sharing the piste and “a slightly doglegged swath of snow” that was “lined with rocks from top to bottom,” although there were no lift lines, he writes.

The chalet, perched on a rocky precipice, was “so frightening and insecure-looking,” that “some skiers refused to enter it,” Frees says. With the altitude nearing 18,000 feet, other visitors didn’t even bother trying, exiting the minibus up from La Paz only to climb into the truck heading back down the road.

This was the electric, eclectic golden period. One 1,000-foot run served by a single rope tow prone to snapping and powered by a truck engine. A handful of foreign visitors and the dedicated group of Club Andino members. A small, warm refugio built on a cliffside, filled with coca tea, quinoa soup, and music. Weekend races and training events for young locals, supporting ski teams who would go on to participate in four consecutive Olympics starting in 1980. And behind this incredible scene was Samuel Mendoza.

“It was frozen all the time,” Mendoza says. “The people said, ‘This is forever. It will never recede.’”

“But little by little, it started to thaw.”

Scientists had been documenting Chacaltaya for decades, but a systematic study of the glacier began in 1991, led in part by Edson Ramírez of the Universidad Mayor de San Andrés in La Paz (UMSA). Glaciologists’ observations began to echo the concerns skiers had voiced for years: Chacaltaya was melting—and fast.

“Snow would fall at night,” Mendoza says, “but it would be gone by midday.” As temperatures rose, the glacier retreated, exposing more and more of the rock underneath.

While the retreat was evident in some of the earliest photos from the 1940s, Ramírez and his team found that, in just six years from 1992 to 1998, the glacier’s melt had accelerated dramatically, losing more than 40% of its surface area and roughly two-thirds of its ice volume. The team’s prediction: The glacier would disappear within 10 to 15 years.

By 2009, the glacier was completely gone.

“The entire glacier of the world’s highest ski slope had turned to water,” Mendoza reflects.

As the ski run melted under them, various last-ditch efforts were implemented to keep the sport alive. Artificial snow production was attempted, but ultimately proved too costly. Moving the resort to other nearby mountains was considered, but transportation and access were constant hurdles. Even traditional Andean rituals were offered to the mountain gods.

But the glacier, once gone, would not come back.

Without their ski hub, the Club Andino eventually unraveled. A photo hangs in the abandoned refugio of smiling members piled outside the club. Mendoza tells me their names—a running list of friends moved abroad or passed away. Even their headquarters in La Paz is now shuttered.

While sooner than expected, Chacaltaya’s glacier death was not unique within the broader scope of Andean glaciers. Research published in 2026 by Giuliana Adrianzen and Andrew Malone of the University of Illinois Chicago found that Bolivia’s Cordillera Real lost a stunning 42% of its glaciated area between 1992 and 2024.

This trend is widespread across the Andes, which are home to 99% of the world’s tropical glacier area—particularly vulnerable ice fields located near the Earth’s equator.

Glaciers in this latitudinal band are much more susceptible to small temperature changes than those outside of it. Kept frozen primarily by extreme altitude, tropical glaciers already exist close to the temperature threshold to sustain permanent ice; they also don’t experience the long, cold winters of glaciers nearer the poles. Andean glaciers are now thinning 35% faster than the global average, according to a 2025 international report co-authored by researchers at the University of Sheffield. As global warming pushes the freezing level higher, more precipitation falls on these glaciers as rain instead of snow, accelerating the melt.

Over the 60 years between 1960 and 2020, Peru lost 56% of its glacier area. In 2024, Venezuela was declared glacier-free with the death of the Humboldt Glacier (named, perhaps ominously, after the German naturalist who pioneered the notion that everything in the natural world is connected). Colombia is following the same trajectory, having lost more than 90% of its glaciated area since the mid-1800s.

According to UNESCO, the Andes could lose 78 to 97% of their tropical glacier volume by the year 2100.

Of course, more than skiing is at risk—including the water supply risk of some 90 million people across the Andes. These glaciers serve as water reserves for the millions of people who live downstream, and their disappearance foreshadows looming ecological disasters. Many Andean municipalities also rely on hydroelectric power, which depends on steady dry-season meltwater from the glaciers. As the glaciers shrink, that flow is dwindling, increasing the severity of droughts.

While Chacaltaya’s lift has long since stopped spinning, a handful of trained guides and foreign clients continue to practice ski mountaineering in Bolivia, climbing high peaks and bombing descents on still-intact glaciers. While the chalet has ceased to function, the mountain remains an active scientific base. The Chacaltaya Observatory, run by UMSA’s Laboratory for Atmospheric Physics—with multiple international collaborators—continues to measure the atmosphere, climate, and cosmic rays.

And although skiing has abandoned the mountain, Mendoza has not.

Since his father died on Chacaltaya over 30 years ago, Mendoza has served as the mountain’s main caretaker, a position he continues to hold. He spends more time in El Alto with his family now, but he and his brother Adolfo still make multiple trips a week to Chacaltaya, welcoming the handful of tourists who come to visit the abandoned chalet or use it as an acclimatization hike. With the small collected entrance fees, he pays for repairs and maintains his memories of the resort.

Many of Mendoza’s days, however, are spent in solitude, standing alone at 17,000 feet on Chacaltaya’s rocky remains.

“When you’re alone it’s a little sad,” he says. “With only the birds, the condors, the Andean foxes.”

Since the collapse of the glacier, a new group of athletes has taken to Chacaltaya: trail runners—whose arrival is directly tied to skiing’s disappearance. Paolo Choque is the director of skyrunning for the Bolivian Ski and Mountaineering Federation. One of the “last people to learn to ski in Bolivia,” Choque witnessed the collapse of skiing at Chacaltaya, and he has since helped cultivate trail running to take its place.

In 2001, when Choque learned to ski, the main chunk of the glacier was already “ruined,” he says. Against the backdrop of the dying mountain, Choque became involved in promoting skiing and snowboarding in Bolivia, including searching for alternative mountains to host competitions.

In 2011, the federation found another suitable slope at nearby Charquini and hosted a Bolivian Ski Championship. Choque says that snowboarding grew in popularity over a handful of years with the promotion efforts, but participation numbers remained low—with just 25 racers in the snowboard event in 2015. Amid melting ice and low participation, he made the decision to pivot. “I said, ‘No, this isn’t going anywhere. We don’t even have a ski slope.’”

Inspired by the sport’s explosion in Spain, Choque organized a pilot skyrunning race on Chacaltaya in 2016, which was met with a strong reception. Athletes had returned to the mountain. The federation’s championship now draws about 200 participants each year, according to Choque. Racers gain points at multiple events across the country, which take place over otherworldly terrain—from the world’s largest salt flats in Uyuni to the folds of the Sajama stratovolcano, the shores of Lake Titicaca, and, of course, Chacaltaya Mountain.

“Skiing may have died,” Choque says, “but mountain sports have not.”

While private trail races have also increased in popularity in Bolivia over the past decade, the federation aims to develop skyrunning and its next generation of athletes through accessible competition. Race entries, Choque emphasizes, are kept inexpensive, and youth competition categories give athletes the opportunity to qualify for international competition.

“For me, sport must come first, and it must be accessible to everyone,” Choque says.

Despite challenges with funding, Choque says the federation has seen success in sending participants to compete in the South American Championships, where they have earned podium finishes, including three medals in 2025.

As one sport fades and another grows, Choque defines what success could look like for Bolivian skyrunning.

“What I want to achieve is to bring a South American championship here, and if possible, even a youth world championship to Bolivia,” he says. “We have the potential.”

Paolo and the federation hope that Chacaltaya will continue to be an important mountain hub for decades to come—with or without the glacier.

For all of the uniqueness of Chacaltaya’s history, it does mirror a larger global skiing trend: most of the participants were wealthy. Mendoza remembers well the divide caused by the cost of equipment. “From the city of El Alto there weren’t a lot of skiers,” he says.

Through the Ski and Mountaineering Federation, Choque is determined that the next iteration of Chacaltaya’s mountain sports—trail and sky running—do not follow the same pattern. Mendoza, meanwhile, has seen some of the runners who are taking to the mountain to train where he once skied. I ask him if he would ever run one of the races, and he tells me he enjoys running. His knees, though, keep him from doing too much of it. But when a German tourist wanted to race from the summit to the lagoon below, Mendoza happily said yes.

“Replacing skiing at Chacaltaya in the future is possible,” he says.

Looking across the dry slope where he learned to ski, the rusted remains of his rope tow, the faded chalet and the memories contained, Mendoza takes a deep breath. At the end of the day, as we drive the winding dirt road down to the city with Chacaltaya shrinking into the distance behind us, he looks ahead.

“It makes me happy when people visit the mountain,” he says.
