#8178. The Best Gifts for Overlanders Who Love to Explore Off-Road

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Overlanding is a pretty niche activity, so it can be hard to find the perfect gift for the driver in your life. Fear not. As an overlander myself, I’ve compiled a comprehensive gift list that has suggestions for overland rookies and veterans alike. I’ve included a wide range of price options, with some gift ideas so big they’ll take up half your living room and others small enough to fit under the tree.

Tires are the most important overland upgrade. A good set of all-terrain tires like the BFGoodrich KO3s helps drivers safely get through snow and mud, and up and down rocky backcountry roads. Their tougher construction also helps resist flats. I love the KO3s for their legendary off-road reliability combined with their quiet ride on pavement.

Overlanders love to get stuck so they can get back out, which makes recovery gear essential. Maxtrax boards slip under tires that have lost traction, allowing the vehicle to slowly inch out of snow, mud, sand, or whatever else it’s bogged down in. Go for the more expensive Xtreme version because it comes with metal traction teeth that last significantly longer.

Airing down tires is often the easiest way to get unstuck because it increases the tires’ contact patch. I love the Rhino kit because it airs down four tires at once. I also recommend this ARB air compressor that attaches to a car battery and can reinflate the tires before you hit pavement again.

Sometimes self-recovery isn’t an option after getting stuck, and I’ve had to get yanked out by a friend. This device fits in the two-inch rear receiver on any truck or SUV and creates a safe place to attach a D-ring and recovery strap. Heads up: Make sure whoever you gift this to knows how to use it properly before heading out.

Folded down, this shovel is only 18 inches long. Fully extended, it goes to 34 inches and is perfect for digging your truck out of a snowbank or excavating a cathole near camp. I’ve tested an earlier version of this shovel for years, and the carbon steel head has put up with rocks, trees, and firm ground without ever bending or chipping.

Anyone who’s overlanding for more than a couple of days will love an electric fridge. It eliminates ice runs and keeps food from drowning in meltwater. Dometic makes some of the most reliable fridges on the market. I like this one because it has two zones: one a fridge, the other either a fridge or a freezer.

Coffee tastes better at 9,000 feet. To brew it there, Yeti’s indestructible French press is my go-to. I’ve thrown it in a kitchen box or just let it roll around in the back of my truck, and it still works perfectly every time. I also love that it has a ceramic lining so the coffee doesn’t taste like metal.

Water can be a precious commodity on a backcountry trip. That’s why I use this battery-powered faucet that pulls water from a jug and then dispenses just the right amount so I can wash my hands or do dishes. One charge lasts for weeks, and all the hoses are easy to clean at home. Pair it with a Dometic water jug for the ideal setup.

The REDARC GoBlock is my go-to overland battery (for fridges, lights, etc.) because it’s designed to be charged in multiple ways. I can connect solar panels to add juice at camp, or I can wire it to my alternator so it gets topped off while I’m driving. I recommend the kit version, which includes a dock that bolts to a truck bed and gives the battery a secure place to live at all times.

iKamper nailed the details with this version of the Skycamp rooftop tent. It has the smartest mounting system I’ve tested. The bombproof hardshell cover will put up with years of sun and weather, and inside it’s extra roomy thanks to a clever tent design. It’s pricey, but this is one of those buy-once, cry-once purchases that you’ll have for at least a decade.

Two layers of enhanced memory foam make the Foamy the most comfortable camping mat on the market. Nothing else I’ve tested even comes close. Perfect for larger tents or truck beds, the Foamy almost guarantees a good night’s sleep because it’s so plush. Pair it with a camping blanket and the setup will be almost as comfortable as what you’re used to at home.

Overlanding requires a lot of gear. The best way to keep it all organized is a Kitworks Gear Box. Infinitely customizable, the Gear Box is the perfect storage method for a camp kitchen, recovery gear, dry food, even clothing. Made from honeycomb panels covered in a 900-denier ripstop shell, the box has proven just as durable as any hard-sided competitor.

Don’t invest in a dash-mounted radio—get two of these instead. With an ultra-reliable, multi-day battery and huge range, these radios are the best way to stay in touch with buddies when cell phones don’t work. When I’m not using the radios in my truck, I use them to keep in contact while backcountry skiing, hunting, and other off-grid adventures.

#8177. After a Scathing Report on the Dragon Bravo Fire, the Grand Canyon’s Superintendent Is Retiring

Smoke rises from the Dragon Bravo Fire on the Grand Canyon’s North Rim in July 2025. The wildfire burned more than 145,000 acres and destroyed 114 structures, including the historic Grand Canyon Lodge (Photo: slovegrove/Getty)

On November 23, Grand Canyon National Park Superintendent Ed Keable announced his plan to retire at the end of 2026, after more than six years overseeing the park.

“As Geoffrey Chaucer wrote, ‘All good things must come to an end.’ So, too, my time at GRCA,” Keable wrote in a November 23 email to park employees obtained by Arizona Public Radio station KNAU. In the email, he confirmed that his last day will be December 31 and that agency leaders are working to identify an acting superintendent to take over on January 1.

Keable’s announcement came just ten days after the Department of the Interior released a damning 65-page investigative report detailing how leadership failures, inadequate preparation, and communication breakdowns contributed to the devastating 2025 Dragon Bravo Fire, which destroyed 114 structures on the park’s North Rim, including the historic Grand Canyon Lodge.

The investigation drew on interviews with more than 70 people and a review of over 18,000 documents, including fire management plans and communication logs.

Keable’s retirement email made no mention of the Dragon Bravo Fire or the Interior Department’s investigative report.

“I have made this decision for very personal reasons,” Keable wrote.

Outside contacted Keable and the National Park Service for comment but did not receive a response as of the publishing of this story.

A career government attorney, Keable spent 23 years in the Interior Department’s Office of the Solicitor, including eight years as assistant solicitor of general law, before his appointment in April 2020 during President Donald Trump’s first administration. He had no previous experience working for the National Park Service.

The Coalition to Protect America’s National Parks, an organization representing current and former park service employees, issued a statement on April 3, 2020, criticizing Keable’s selection the same day the NPS announced his appointment.

“Ed Keable is not qualified to manage and lead a complicated park such as the Grand Canyon,” Phil Francis, then-chair of the coalition, said in the statement.

In the appointment announcement, NPS Deputy Director David Vela praised Keable’s leadership abilities and cited his experience within the Interior Department as an asset to the park.

Sparked by lightning on July 4, 2025, the Dragon Bravo Fire burned more than 145,000 acres over nearly three months and cost an estimated $141 million to suppress, according to the federal report. Investigators concluded that “the most consequential drivers were not environmental,” finding that many of the challenges the NPS and firefighters encountered during the blaze were “foreseeable, preventable, and reflective of broader institutional issues.”

In the report, investigators determined that “leadership roles did not align with expertise or decision making authority.” As the fire’s agency administrator, Keable was responsible for overseeing firefighting strategy and authorizing suppression tactics.

Under NPS guidelines, superintendents at wildfire-prone parks are expected to qualify for that role within two years of their appointment. Five years into his tenure, Keable still lacked that qualification, the report said. Although qualified administrators were available locally, the park didn’t bring one in until July 30, nearly four weeks after the fire ignited.

Keable initially approved a strategy known as confine and contain, which involves keeping a wildfire within designated boundaries rather than extinguishing it entirely. The approach conflicted with 2025 federal guidance against managing wildfires for ecological benefit, though investigators indicated that Keable had not received that, the report said.

Park leadership reaffirmed the strategy twice over the next five days, during which the fire breached planned containment lines.

“Continued authorization of the confine and contain strategy did not reflect awareness of changing conditions or escalating risk,” investigators wrote.

Communication failures also delayed firefighters’ efforts to slow the blaze using aerial fire retardant. Keable authorized retardant drops on July 13, once an earlier request from firefighters was clarified, but by then, the Grand Canyon Lodge had already burned.

The report stopped short of assigning individual fault. “The Dragon Bravo Fire should be understood as a warning event,” the report stated. “The findings demonstrate outcomes were shaped less by tactical execution than by NPS systemic issues related to authority, qualifications, and decision processes.”

As Outside reported in April, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum suggested that full suppression might have prevented hundreds of millions of dollars in property losses, though wildland firefighters noted that the canyon’s steep terrain initially made ground operations unsafe.

The National Park Service advertised Keable’s position on November 24, with applications closing December 8 and an annual salary ranging from $162,740 to $228,000. Responsibilities include overseeing wildland firefighting, emergency medical services, and backcountry rescues.

The job hunt comes at a pressing time for the national park. A devastating flash flood on August 29 destroyed trails and infrastructure along the Colorado River and led to three deaths. Facilities on the South Rim went without running water for nearly two months until the park restored water service to six lodges on November 20.

Among the next superintendent’s biggest challenges will be rebuilding the North Rim. Earlier this month, the park service concluded a public comment period on three preliminary redevelopment concepts for the area. Congress is also considering the North Rim Restoration Act, which would give the park service greater contracting flexibility to expedite reconstruction.

Sections of the fire-damaged North Rim reopened to visitors in May, but the August flash flood hindered reconstruction efforts, washing out trails and damaging bridges and critical infrastructure. The entire North Kaibab Trail and Cottonwood Campground remain closed, and Phantom Ranch’s lodging closure has been extended through January 31, 2027.

#8176. How to Crew an Ultramarathon Like a Pro

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Addison Smith is an ultrarunning coach at CTS, one of the most popular and accomplished coaching organizations in endurance sports. He’s headed up the CTS team’s crewing logistics and efforts for races like the Western States 100 and Leadville 100 for years, helping athletes land multiple podium finishes, course records, and Golden Tickets.

Crewing a runner at a trail race may seem like a simple task and, in a lot of ways, it is. But in the thick of the moment, it can also be stressful, chaotic, and leave you feeling powerless in a situation you hadn’t prepared for. I’ve crewed at a wide variety of trail and ultra races for both cutoff chasers and elite athletes alike. For the past four years, I’ve led the Carmichael Training Systems (CTS) crewing operations for our team crewing efforts at the Western States 100, Javelina 100, Leadville 100, and Canyons Endurance Events. Each race has its own flavor of support, from the rules on the type of assistance you can give, to how frequently you can assist, and how many members each crew can have.

Ultrarunning really is a team sport, and the proficiency of the crew can be the difference between winning or losing, finishing or DNFing. I’ve seen crew talk a discouraged and fatigued but physically healthy athlete into quitting because they weren’t confident in how to help them through their low patch. I’ve also seen a well-treated blister and some words of encouragement get an athlete back on their pacing plan after a few miles of spiraled thoughts and painful steps.

The following is a framework for streamlining the crewing process. It’s less a gear guide on what’s in my blister kit and the type of power bank I like using, and more about preparing you to organize and ask the right questions so you can crew with confidence when your runner is depending on you.

Crewing is a selfless act of caring for a runner. But, paradoxically, it requires a deliberate effort of self-care by the members of the crew as well. For anyone who has crewed a race that lasts most of the day—if not multiple days—you know just how mentally and physically fatiguing an endeavor it can be. You may not be physically running the race, but you’re trying to juggle logistical details—often sleep deprived and outside in harsh conditions. With so many moving pieces, crew members often forget to drink or eat enough themselves—which can show up in the way they communicate or execute their role. Remember that, although some of the tips and tasks outlined below can be time-consuming, the additional organization will hopefully relieve stress, save time, and improve not only your availability for your athlete, but also your enjoyment of the crewing experience.

Crews of various sizes can be successful. In general, three people is ideal in most scenarios for efficiency and effectiveness. The first crew member can focus on restocking fuel, hydration, and equipment. The second crew member can focus on tending to the athlete directly. They will be the main communicator; giving advice and reassurance, while also tending to their immediate physical needs like cooling or blisters. The third crew member is the pacer. Their primary job is preparing themselves for the long stretch of miles they will run with the athlete by taking care of themselves throughout the day, resting, fueling, and saving energy before their run.

Specific races would certainly require more crew. For example, the Badwater 135 is a great example of a race where four crew members would be ideal. Crew vehicles are required to follow each athlete along the course, and crews are allowed to pace athletes after Stovepipe Wells (Mile 42). If two people are tasked with driving and pacing, having another crew member ready to cool the athlete and swap bottles every few miles keeps the frequent need for crewing in the hot temperatures efficient. Not to mention having a fourth crew member to fill in and take turns allows crew members to rest and stay fresh in a race that typically takes more than 35 hours to complete.

While three to four person crews are ideal, they may not be a possibility for some athletes. I know many couples who crew their significant other by themselves in 100 mile races—often to great success. If you find yourself in a single-person crew situation, most races have a multitude of helpful volunteers at aid stations that can assist you in crewing when needed. Three to four prepared crew members may give the best chance to be as efficient through an aid station as possible, but it certainly isn’t an absolute necessity for success.

I would define crewing as people meeting an athlete at aid stations during a race to give physical and emotional support to help them accomplish their race goals. The distinction between physical and emotional support provides the general framework I use to prepare to crew effectively. The physical support could be boiled down to efficient problem solving and transitions, and the emotional side of things to empowering interactions (or a psychological pick-me-up). As crew members, we have an opportunity to give physical support (fueling, hydration, gear, cooling, etc.), as well as emotional support (acknowledgement, guidance, tone, motivation, etc.). You can be incredibly organized as a crew, but if you give the wrong emotional support, it could affect your athlete’s race just as much—if not more—than not being prepared with the proper equipment or nutrition. You need to be prepared for both sides of the crewing process to give both yourself and your athlete the best experience possible.

Below, I’ll break down my guidelines to being both physically and emotionally supportive for your athlete.

Though this might seem like the most straightforward tip, it’s the one that requires the most planning beforehand. When crewing, you need to prepare  by having the right tools and gear for a variety of situations your athlete might find themselves in–whether that’s dealing with heat, high altitude, an upset stomach, blisters, heat, cold, or any number of other issues.  Here’s a checklist of essential gear that CTS coaching uses at the majority of trail and ultra races we crew:

Going into the race, it’s important to know how your athlete’s preparation went in the lead-up, what their goals are for the race, as well as their pacing, fueling, hydration, and gear strategies. Once the race starts, it’s equally important to collect real-time information via timing splits or from other crew members. This information gives you a clearer picture of how the race is going, and helps you anticipate what might be needed at the next crewing opportunity.

Below is what we refer to as an “athlete tracking card”. It is an easy-to-use document that summarizes the necessary context of crewing, so when it’s 2 a.m. and you can’t juggle all of the information needed, you’re still able to reorient yourself around the most important details. Whether you’re a first time crew member or an experienced one, I strongly recommend creating your own version of this card to correctly orient yourself around the critical contextual information for the specific athlete and race demands.

The last piece to successful physical crewing is effective communication between crew members. Sometimes crewing is a one-person job, but that usually isn’t the case. Ultras often require multiple people to handle various tasks like driving, pacing, cooling, nutrition, etc. The more you can delegate roles–and stick to those roles–the more efficient you can be getting an athlete in and out of the aid station. Once a role has been assigned within the group, it’s up to that person to own their role. In other words, each person should know what gear they need. For example, the person in charge of cooling should know where the bucket, water, and ice are. Each person should also take the initiative to ask the athlete ahead of time how they want the task performed. If you’re in charge of bottles, nutrition, or an athlete’s pack, you should know exactly where they want each item. Owning your role also allows for a more efficient and less stressful pivot if something goes awry.

In all of my experience at races watching athlete and crew scenarios play out, this is the aspect of crewing that is most easily mishandled. Let’s dive into a race scenario:

You’re racing the Leadville 100 and the second summit of Hope Pass is in your rearview mirror. You’ve been at 10,000 feet or more for most of the day, you’re tired, under-fueled, slightly dehydrated, and you’ve rallied through some stomach issues. The sun is finally starting to go down and the temperatures are dropping. Your muscles ache and you’re starting to get a hot spot on your foot, but you’re still moving fairly well just behind your goal pace. You can’t wait to get to the Twin Lakes inbound aid station to see your crew, and you’re excited to pick up your pacer. When you get to the aid station, your crew waves you into your tent. You tell them you haven’t been able to get food down consistently, you’re developing hot spots, you don’t want to take in gels anymore, and the planned electrolyte mix sounds terrible now. You ask what you should try. The crew turns to each other, perplexed, saying, “This wasn’t in the plan, what do we do now?” For the next five minutes, the crew peppers you with a dozen different options you could try. “Maybe change your shoes,” one crew member says. Another chimes in “maybe just change your socks or try those ‘toe condoms,’ I read that they work great.” Instead of one clear solution, you’re given a dozen half-baked ideas for each ailment, and with each passing minute the tone is getting sharper between the crew members, realizing they were supposed to get you out of the aid station minutes ago. You finally make a decision on what hydration and fueling options you’re pivoting to, and decide to change your socks and get out of the aid station. While your crew got you some fresh equipment and nutrition, you’ve also picked up some newfound anxiety and uncertainty.

Bottom line: Crew with calm confidence. If you’re prepared to pivot, there’s less to do on the fly. And when you don’t have a good answer to a mild medical problem, have someone calmly but efficiently go over to the medical staff or aid station captain to ask for advice.

Acting as a positive light to a runner who likely has experienced a full spectrum of emotions throughout an ultra is crucial. When someone is fatigued, it is easy to wear their emotions on their sleeve. And when things aren’t going particularly well, it’s very easy to think that things are going worse than they actually are. If you can not only be a voice of reason, but also lift an athlete’s spirits while doing so, you can help them reframe their current situation, thus helping them start to build positive momentum. CTS coaches like to use this saying with athletes in a crewing context: “It doesn’t always get worse.” It’s my favorite way to help an athlete reframe their current situation and share a positive sentiment. While acknowledging the current scenario may not be ideal, the trail ahead is an unknown, and that unknown has the possibility of being positive in the future.

Effective communication is not only important for physical support, but emotional support as well. At each crewing opportunity, start by asking yourself these  questions before jumping into action:

Whether the athlete needs you to give them some tough love or to be their biggest cheerleader, having a calm demeanor, bringing positive energy, and being an effective communicator can turn a DNF into a salvaged race they can be proud of for years to come.

Crewing’s a simple task but requires a lot of preparation both before and during the event. The more you do it, the more comfortable and efficient you’ll get at it. The long days at Foresthill, Javelina Jeadquarters, and Champex-Lac preparing for an athlete’s arrival and executing a top-notch crewing job is one of the most satisfying things I do as a coach. I hope this framework gives you new perspectives on how to best go about crewing, a few more things to add to your gear list, and helps you enjoy the process of crewing more by knowing that you’re prepared and making the right decisions each step of the way.

#8175. How I Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Free Rider’ on El Cap in 18.5 Hours

Left to right: Alex Honnold, Connor Herson, and Tommy Caldwell take a celebratory selfie at the top of 'The Prophet' on El Cap. (Photo: Courtesy of Alex Honnold)

My alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start. I’ve got half an hour to pull myself together before Alex gets here and we start hiking. As I choke down breakfast, I can’t help but wonder if I’m in over my head. Despite Alex and Tommy’s best reassurances, The Prophet scares me.

Established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes. Indeed, it’s broken a few bones over the years, and to this day, Leo and Jason’s ground up attempt remains one of the boldest and most heroic chapters in El Cap’s history. Growing up, I always told myself that I’d never climb The Prophet. Maybe I’d rap into the A1 Beauty (the splitter crux pitch, rated 5.13d, though Leo, Sonnie Trotter, and Alex have all talked of upgrading it to 5.14a1) to try it, but the rest of the route was too dangerous for me—I don’t do dangerous stuff.

I wasn’t particularly surprised when Alex Honnold and Tommy Caldwell started trying The Prophet this season, but I watched their progress as a friend and spectator, not a potential suitor for the route. My own project on Leaning Tower was taking all my time this season.

On November 11, while eating breakfast and preparing for a day on my project, I ran into Alex and congratulated him on his send. He was hiking up that afternoon to belay Tommy, who was four days into his send push and trying the A1 Beauty. Alex offered to jumar and belay me on a ground-up push the next day, promising that the route was safer with his beta. I joked that I’d take him up if I couldn’t find a partner the next day for my project.

I had a very promising session on my project, but that afternoon, I was still partnerless for the following day, so I called up Alex to ask if his offer was still valid. In between Tommy’s redpoint goes on the A1, Alex called me back to tell me what gear I’d need. We planned to start climbing around 4:00 a.m. the following morning.

Packing up that evening, I felt wholly unprepared. I’d been sport climbing all summer and hadn’t done more than about six pitches in a day since spring. The only valley granite I’d touched this season was my overhanging, physical project on Leaning Tower, which was almost certainly a different style from the slabby, polished, and technical El Cap granite ahead of me. I’d need to re-adapt efficiently and quickly, working with a lower stamina threshold than I was used to.

Hiking up the following morning on November 12, Alex started breaking down the route for me. He told me how he and Tommy had cleaned all the pitches, how they ticked and recorded every gear placement. As I started leading the first few pitches, I realized just how helpful this was going to be: I took only the exact rack I’d need for each pitch, and I didn’t have to stress at all about beta or gear. I took Alex at his word about the relative safety of each section (a risky decision, I know…) and tried to turn my brain off to the fullest extent possible.

I settled into a sort of flow state; with the darkness obscuring any large runouts and Alex reassuring me of each gear placement ahead of me, I climbed calmly and intentionally over the lower pitches of the route. I couldn’t fathom Leo and Jason coming up here to find loose rock, grass-filled cracks, and no obvious route. It was certainly a far cry from my own experience on the freshly cleaned and ticked route. I remained relatively calm even over pitches four through six, the first few 5.13 pitches.

As we climbed higher and dawn broke, we saw Tommy above us; he’d not quite sent the night before, but he’d decided to spend another night on the wall and watch my attempt in the morning. With Tommy’s encouragement, I climbed the Guillotine Pitch (pitch eight, 5.13b), then the Devil’s Reacharound (pitch nine, 5.13a). Before long, I joined him at his portaledge at the base of the A1 Beauty just as the morning sun hit. What a perfect splitter it looked like, too—everything I could ever want in a pitch, at the very top of El Cap.

The A1 Beauty sees direct sun from first light until sunset, and it bakes. It was already quite warm, and I figured it would only get warmer as the day progressed. Without much waiting, I racked up and started what I thought would be a beta sussing mission. A few moves in, I realized this attempt could be more than just that; with Tommy hanging on a static rope above me, telling me exactly what to do, I found myself through the low crux (~V8), then through the next section. As I got higher and higher, I tried to push down the feeling that I might just pull it off on this first attempt and instead focus on each move, each foothold, each gear placement. It felt perfect. Before I knew it, I was at the next anchor, absolutely thrilled.

As excited as I was about the A1, suddenly the route became much more intense. I was only two pitches below the summit. Two pitches from flashing the entire route in a day. Two pitches from an El Cap flash. The following pitch was easy enough, but the exit pitch intimidated me: a 13b boulder problem right off the belay, involving an insecure standup on poor footholds.

I climbed up to the boulder and back down to the belay a few times, feeling increasingly nervous. Eventually, I went for it: I placed the foot, took a deep breath, and stood. The foot held, and I excitedly reached for the next hold, which guards easier climbing to the top. I briefly lost focus, allowing a small voice to say, I’m doing it! It’s happening! The next thing I knew, my foot had slipped and I was hanging on the rope. My flash go was botched.

At that moment, I lost all perspective of the incredible morning of climbing I’d had; I was devastated. Half an hour later, topping out The Prophet after successfully climbing the pitch, I felt the most hollow I’ve felt upon topping out El Cap. Alex and Tommy joined me on top. As they packed their haulbag and portaledge, I couldn’t help but regret my missed opportunity.

Within a few minutes, however, I regained some perspective. It had been an incredibly memorable morning of climbing, and I’d still freed The Prophet ground-up in about seven hours. Only that morning, doing this would have been a dream come true, and I smiled a bit. I checked the time: 11:30 a.m. “Wow! I can drive home and meet my family in time for dinner!” I laughed and joked to Tommy and Alex.

Alex turned and gave me a wry smile. “You know, you could do a Double right now. Compared to The Prophet, Free Rider will probably feel pretty easy.”

Tommy pitched in: “Yeah, I’d jug Free Rider this afternoon if you want!”

I stopped sorting my gear and stared. Great. I’m getting peer pressured by my heroes.

Among the rules I live by is that if Alex or Tommy offers something, I don’t turn them down. Especially a support mission on El Cap. As tired and emotionally drained as I was, I reminded myself just how much I’ve wanted to do the El Cap Double my entire life. I remembered topping out the free Nose-in-a-day last year, when I called every climber in the Valley to see if I could find a partner for a Double that day, to no avail. This sort of opportunity doesn’t come around particularly often. Even as I waffled about whether to go for it, the decision had been made. In a few hours’ time, I knew I’d be starting up Freeblast.

The climbing on Free Rider is significantly easier than on The Prophet, and I’d done most of the pitches when I freed the Salathé in 2022. I knew there would be little suspense about whether I’d be physically capable of sending it. However, I also knew I wasn’t in big walling shape, and besides, this would be far and away the most pitches I’ve climbed in a day. I remember watching the video of Tommy freeing the El Cap double back in 2005, where he nearly lost it at the Enduro Corner. I wondered if I was in for a similar bout.

The first few pitches on Free Rider went remarkably smoothly. Alex, still keen on supporting me, had jugged our day pack up the Heart Lines, which made Freeblast an absolute breeze. My feet were hurting, but I could feel the ibuprofen I’d pounded at the base starting to kick in. I settled into a flow, and pitch after pitch flew past. I felt remarkably fresh. With Tommy’s encouragement and psych, I was optimistic.

Around the Monster Offwidth (pitch 20 of 30 on Free Rider), darkness fell. I could feel the fatigue building; our pace slowed, but we kept moving. I was making a conscious effort to stay positive and cheerful, to act like I had endless energy in the hopes that I could fake that energy into existence.

When we reached the crux, I opted for the Teflon Corner instead of the Boulder Problem. I’d never tried the Boulder before, and I didn’t want my first attempt to be 40-odd pitches into the day. The Teflon went down on my first try, and before long, we were at the Enduro Corner. Tommy suggested that I skip the hanging belay at the end of the Enduro Corner and link it into the Round Table Traverse. I rolled my eyes, thinking that I’d be lucky to scrape my way up the Corner on its own, but to my surprise, I felt remarkably fresh. I reached the hanging belay and kept climbing, thankful to have cleared that last hurdle.

At 10:45 p.m., a little more than eight hours after starting Free Rider and 18.5 hours after starting up The Prophet, Tommy and I topped out to strong, cold winds. We didn’t stick around long to celebrate; already shivering, we quickly packed and started running to stay warm on the hike down. As we got lower and warmed up, however, we slowed down and soaked in the unforgettable day we’d just had: around 45 pitches of climbing for a free El Cap Double!

Alex and Tommy both have families. They both had good reason to rush home ahead of the incoming storm instead of supporting some kid who wanted to try their project. And to be honest, I wouldn’t have blamed them if they didn’t want me to mooch off their hard work prepping The Prophet. There’s absolutely no way I could have done The Prophet ground up and in a day without the labor Tommy and Alex spent to find the route, clean loose rock, and find all the gear beta. After four days on the wall and away from his family, I would have completely understood if Tommy wanted to get home to his kids rather than go up El Cap a second time that day—especially with Tioga Pass imminently closing, which meant supporting me on Free Rider would lengthen his drive home by about an hour.

Nevertheless, their support that day exemplifies the exact values I love to see in climbing. This is the sport I want climbing to be: one where the giants, the biggest legends of the game, are generous enough to go out of their way to help younger up-and-comers. A sport where the younger generation is not seen as a fresh wave of competition but is instead embraced and mentored.

Not flashing The Prophet is certainly going to sting for a while. I still replay that moment on the exit pitch daily, and I’m sure I’ll always feel some regret about it. Still, the more I reflect on that day, the more Alex and Tommy’s support stands out to me. Every outing leaves us with a lesson or slightly shifted worldview. In 10 or 20 years, I’m confident that looking back on the El Cap Double will remind me that there is a world larger than my own climbing; that, like Tommy and Alex, I can make another climber’s entire season by simply offering them a few hours of my time and a bit of encouragement. As I grow and find my place in the climbing world, I can only hope to be as influential a mentor to future generations.

1It’s hard to guess after only one attempt, but I wouldn’t argue with 5.14a for that pitch! I also could see upper-end 5.13d, though.

#8174. She Asked the Appalachian Trail Conservancy to Start an Artist Residency. Now You Can Apply, Too.

When Philadelphia metalsmith Mallory “Bullseye” Weston wanted to apply for an artist residency on the Appalachian Trail, she ran into a problem. They didn’t have one.

So she sent a cold email. Within a few hours, Dakota Jackson, senior director of visitor engagement at the Appalachian Trail Conservancy (ATC) had written back to set up a meeting. It was perfect timing: The ATC was approaching its centennial in 2025 and looking for new ways to get more hikers on trail. As Caroline Ralston, the ATC’s associate vice president of marketing and communications, put it, “at that time, we realized we didn’t really have anything for creatives.”

From her Philadelphia studio, Weston had a sense of what a good walk could yield. She’d already put in miles on the John Muir Trail (JMT), the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT), and the Tahoe Rim Trail, and was starting to see a clearer connection between her creative life and her hiking.

A 454-mile stretch of the PCT found its way into 30 titanium brooches shaped like lengths of paracord. Their colors and patterns changed with her mood on the trail, day by day. Her stories became a zine. So when she and Jackson started talking through possible structures for the ATC’s inaugural artist in residence program, she offered herself up as the guinea pig.

Last year, when the Conservancy officially launched the program, Weston set out from Georgia as its pilot creative. “Almost a year after I planted the seed for this wild idea, somehow, things came together to make it a reality,” Weston wrote in her blog.

Since metalwork is specialized and far from portable, she used the hike as an inspiration gathering exercise rather than a time to actually create work. She couldn’t haul a forge, but she could carry a camera. Back in Philadelphia, she’s been picking through her thousands of photographs, taking another look at the pile of butterfly wings she came across, or the blazes she passed.

“Hiking the trail as the ATC’s Artist in Residence has motivated me to be more observant of my surroundings,” Weston told the ATC. “I’ve been actively documenting the experience through photography and journaling, wanting to remember the rich details of my hike and use them to generate artwork from the vivid text and images I’ve collected.”

Weston had one piece finished before she ever set foot on the AT. For the trail’s centennial, she designed an enamel pin that hikers could pick up at a visitor center.

The ATC is now looking for its 2027 Artist in Residence, and artists working in any medium have until January 3, 2027, to apply. The residency includes a limited stipend for transportation and lodging for events along the AT, and a two- to four-week stay at Maine’s Monson Arts, an arts center in the last town NOBO hikers pass through before the 100-Mile wilderness. Weston spent five months walking the entire AT, but the next resident could hike a section or spend their time in one town along the trail; the residency’s structure is malleable.

“This program is a new way to experience the trail,” says Ralston. “When the trail was first conceptualized over 100 years ago, one of the founding ideas was that people need a place to escape, connect with nature, and unplug. This program is an extension of that. We want to invite artists to immerse themselves on the trail, connect with nature, and see what kind of inspiration comes from it.”

Along with a résumé or CV and five to 10 work samples, applicants must provide an artist statement and a work proposal. The ATC wants to know what you make, what time on the trail might bring to your work, and how you’d share it.

What makes an application stand out? For Ralston, notable applications will express “a desire to get out there, and a desire to share it publicly.” For Weston, that meant giving talks at trail centers.

Her advice to the next applicant? Think about what a stretch of time on this particular trail might change about the work you already do, and leave yourself some room to be surprised. For Weston, one of those surprises came in her first week out of Georgia.

The first time Weston spotted pink lady’s slipper orchids on the AT, her husband was hiking with her. He’d come along for the first stretch and they saw a few patches together that week. Each flower had a little pouch that she found “kind of weird and grotesque looking, but also very beautiful.” By the time she came across a whole field of them, her husband had gone home to Philadelphia. “I’m all alone, and here’s all these orchids,” she remembers thinking.

Now, back in her Philadelphia studio, she’s working on a recreation of a pink lady’s slipper. Of all the things she saw in five months on trail, that one made what she calls a “one to one translation” into her work.

“Now that I’m back in Philadelphia, I’m distilling all of that experience into work that emerges from it,” says Weston.

#8172. Kiprun Kipsummit Race Review: We Tested the Trail Super Shoe That Won the 2026 Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

When Blandine L’Hirondel crossed the finish line first at the 2026 Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc, the buzz was not only about her record-breaking 21:54:49 but also about what shoes she was wearing. L’Hirondel is a name the trail running world knows well. Her sponsor, Kiprun, isn’t, especially in the United States. Kiprun is the running brand of Decathlon, the French sporting goods giant, and the shoe on L’Hirondel’s feet was its first carbon-plated trail racer, the Kipsummit Race.

The debut racer, also the least expensive shoe on the podium at $250, clearly held its own in a field of tried-and-proven competitors. Runner-up Rachel Entrekin’s Norda 055, for example, retails for $325. Other models on the podium ranged from $260 to $280.

For the last three months, I’ve been testing the Kiprun Kipsummit Race to find out firsthand what this new $250 trail super shoe can do.

Weight: 9 oz (men’s 8); 7.8 oz (women’s 5) Stack Height: 37.5–31.5 mm Heel-to-Toe Drop: 6 mm Lug Depth: 4 mm

+ One of the lightest carbon trail racers + Firm, responsive midsole doesn’t feel mushy + Confidence-inspiring stability and grip, especially on descents – Stiff sole and upper need a break-in period – Not ideal for very technical, rocky terrain

I was first introduced to Kiprun at The Running Event in December 2025, a trade show for run specialty retailers and brands. I was immediately drawn to the Kipsummit Race, the brand’s marquee carbon-plated trail shoe, and couldn’t wait to test it. Nearly nine months later, Blandine L’Hirondel wore it to her record-setting win at UTMB. Coincidentally (or not?), my sample pair arrived in the mail just after the win.

From the moment I picked it up, the Kipsummit Race felt remarkably light. At 9 ounces for a men’s 8 and 7.8 ounces for a women’s 5, it’s one of the lightest carbon-plated trail shoes you can buy. Fittingly, the only other shoe as lightweight is the Asics Metafuji Trail 2, which Ben Dhiman wore to win the men’s race at UTMB.

The Kipsummit Race has one of the toughest uppers I’ve tested. The patented upper material (a blend of polyester, thermoplastic polyurethane, and polyamide) is lightweight and extremely durable, with a stiff, structured feel that really holds the foot in place once the laces are cinched. It’s not the coziest feel out of the box, but over time, it broke in and felt more comfortable.

Underfoot, the ATPU midsole uses an embedded, full-length, forked carbon fiber plate to create a rigid, rockered sole. Most of the ATPU midsoles I’ve tested have been in road shoes, and tend to be very soft. The Kipsummit Race was not. The shoe felt firmer than I expected during my first test run on a crushed gravel path outside Philadelphia. That wasn’t necessarily a bad thing: It was firm, but it had a responsive pop, and I didn’t notice any sinking into the midsole or instability on stance and push-off.

On another test run in Santa Barbara, California, I climbed about 1,200 feet up a dirt fire road. It was rutted and rocky from water runoff, but the shoe remained stable on the uneven terrain. The firmer midsole, paired with a wide base, felt grounded, and the forked plate, with a cut-out under the heel, kept my foot centered. When I needed to navigate through technical terrain, however, the thick, wide profile and lack of ground feel wasn’t ideal.

The Kipsummit Race really shone on the descent. The Vibram Megagrip Litebase outsole with 4 millimeter lugs gripped loose rock and kitty litter with confidence, while still being mild enough to run on roads for long stretches. I’m not naturally a strong downhill runner, but I felt safe going beyond my comfort zone, which I attribute to the combination of great grip, a firmly stable midsole, a wide base, and a secure upper.

The one thing I didn’t get to test is how comfortable the shoe, with its firmer midsole and stiff upper, feels over ultra distances. The shoe started to break in with more use, so you may need to log more miles in it to feel its true comfort. Kiprun boasts that it holds up for more than 1,000 kilometers (about 620 miles), and given that L’Hirondel trusted one pair for the entire UTMB, that tracks.

Like carbon fiber road racing shoes, carbon fiber trail shoes have a reputation for being made only for fast, strong, competitive runners. That reputation may be earned on the road, but I don’t think it’s true for trail shoes. There isn’t nearly as much research showing that carbon fiber trail shoes provide any performance benefit to trail runners, elite or beginner—the plates function as much for protection and stability as they do for propulsion.

That said, plated trail shoes offer a different running experience than non-plated shoes. If that feels good to you, then wear them. This is my long way of saying that the Kiprun Kipsummit Race is suitable for any runner who likes a stiffer shoe, both in flex and cushioning, that holds up to high mileage. It’s best suited for smooth to moderately technical terrain, and for anything from short trail races to 100-milers.

#8171. How My First Multi-Pitch Climb Became a Midnight Barefoot Epic

On July 4, 2026, Audrey Callaway climbed her first real multi-pitch: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches) in Squamish, B.C. The catch? She didn’t start up pitch one until nearly 9 p.m., thus becoming voluntarily benighted in only the most literal sense of the term. “My story isn’t a disaster!” Callaway explains. “It’s about learning, the tenacity of a little psych, and extremely good company.”

After first getting into the sport at a gym in Chicago, Callaway later moved to upstate New York near the Gunks. Currently, she’s studying forestry at the University of Vermont. “I like trees, I like climbing, I like birds,” she says of her big three hobbies. She’s mostly a boulderer and sport climber who wants to get more into trad climbing. She also works at a climbing gym.

Callaway wanted to share her experience to highlight the growing pains of “doing things poorly the first time”—and how the right partners ease those pains. Below, she shares her story and what others embarking on their first multi-pitch can learn from her experience.

It’s really cool to feel very bad at something again.

I was planning to visit my girlfriend Lucy, who had been in Squamish for the whole summer. Then my best friend Will, who I grew up climbing with at the gym, told me he also happened to be going out to Squamish. I got there a few days before him and did a little bouldering.

When Will got there, he was even more psyched than I was. After bouldering all afternoon, we’re sitting around, playing chess and looking through Lucy’s guidebook when we saw a trad climb that looked so cool: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches).

It was 7 p.m., but the sun didn’t set until around 9 p.m. It was very spur of the moment. We’re just like, “We gotta do this thing.” So we quickly got all our stuff together.

We knew it was going to get dark. It’s not like it snuck up on us. But Lucy had a lot of experience. Will and I didn’t know how to trad climb at this point, although he learned later on that trip. So she’s carrying the team. Afterward, she told me she brought only a single rack so that she could share in our sense of adventure and “empathize with the uncertainty.”

First, we got super lost on the way there. We didn’t get to the base of the climb until like 8:45 p.m., but it was still super bright out.

Very quickly, I realized how bad I was at rope management. I was in the middle, belaying Lucy, and we had two ropes. Routefinding is something that you take for granted when you’ve been climbing outside for a while. I was taking the path of most resistance. There was a pretty solid crack on really good terrain, but I’m newer to crack climbing, so I was not about to put my hands in there and trust that. Instead, I was doing this very sketchy 5.10 slab. Eventually, I started using the crack.

We got up to the first belay and we’re all on top of each other because we don’t really know where to be. Nothing was unsafe, but it was very slow. Lucy started going up this 5.6 very runout slab. But I had looped a knot of rope around where I was belaying. I didn’t realize that until I’d fed out enough of the slack. So I kept shorting her like every five feet. I knew that there was totally a way to fix this, but I don’t know how.

Then the sun set. That’s okay, because we had headlamps—but Lucy’s headlamp was dead. It was funny because before we started climbing, Lucy was like, “Guys, make sure you have your headlamps.” But then when we put them on, she’s like, “Can I actually borrow yours?”

So she took mine, and now I was climbing in the dark on slab. It was very precarious, but beautiful. It felt so scary in the moment. But the town was right there, we’re on the most classic 5.8 ever, and we’re a hundred feet off the ground—it wasn’t actually that scary.

Will and I both had super competitive shoes on. It had been two hours at this point and we’re standing on this slab and our feet were killing us. Every time I left the belay, Will told me he “would lowkey start crying a bit” because he knew he’d have to climb soon, enduring more toe pain. So we both took off our shoes because it’s easier to climb barefoot. Now I was barefoot in the dark on this slab.

Every time we got to a new belay, we tried to make the system better. Lucy was just trying to climb, but we’re shorting her every time. Now Will was in the way. We were right on top of each other.

None of these things were particularly hard challenges. If we knew what we were doing, we could have fixed any one of these problems in 30 seconds. I would get back up to Lucy and she would be like, “Why didn’t you just do this?” Then something else would come up.

At one point, probably around 11:30 p.m., Will got a cam stuck. Lucy’s like, “Try wiggling it.” She told him to pull upward, but he said it was literally impossible. Lucy lowered down and pulled it out, first try. There must have been times like this when Lucy was frustrated, but she never showed it. Will describes Lucy as the most patient person he’s ever met.

We got to the top at midnight. It was hypnotizing on the apron. The lights of town beneath us glowed surreally. I smoked my first cigarette at the top.

I remember walking back and it was really quiet. We got back on the road and our gear’s rattling and the moon’s out. It was so quiet and peaceful.

It was one in the morning when we got back to the campground by the Chief. We didn’t want to be disrespectful with a big light, so we put a headlamp under this pickle jar we had. By the light of this pickle lamp, we ate pickles and cold canned minestrone and asked, “What are we gonna do tomorrow?”

To really be benighted, I would say it has to sneak up on you. It kinda felt like it snuck up on me. Clearly, as a group we were aware it was about to happen. But I was surprised when all of a sudden it was dark and I had no headlamp and was climbing barefoot. It made me feel like a salamander, really in touch with the rock.

Lucy and I did another multi-pitch the next day, and since then I’ve done a couple two-pitch climbs in the Gunks when I got back to New York. I will probably do lots of really awesome multi-pitches in my lifetime that are beautiful and scenic with really hard climbing, but I’m never gonna have another one that bad. I’m never gonna have another first one.

As told to Maya Silver. This story has been edited for length, structure, and clarity.

#8170. Carry Less, Eat Better

Some ultralight thru-hikers swear by going stoveless to save weight and time. But when you don’t cook, you might assume there are a few other things you have to do without: full flavor, fresh ingredients, and a diverse slate of nutrients, to name a few. Cold soaking—the popular method of rehydrating dry or instant food with cold water—lets you ditch the stove, fuel canister, and cook pot. But does it also have to mean compromising on a satisfying meal?

Not necessarily. Going stoveless doesn’t have to be all cold couscous, stale chips, and stray sauce packets. Wild Planet offers ready-to-eat wild tuna bowls that are packed with protein and full of flavor. Featuring wild-caught skipjack tuna and organic ingredients, they’re a nutritious solution for anyone looking to fuel up without the fuel canister.

For the no-cook-curious, Wild Planet’s meals make for an easy transition from stove-cooked, pre-packaged backpacking meals, saving ounces while offering similar—or better—nutritional value and flavor.

Take the Wild Tuna and Red Bean Bowl, for example. It’s a tasty combination of skipjack tuna, organic beans, sweetcorn, red peppers, carrots, and spices in organic extra virgin olive oil. It offers 290 calories, with 18 grams of protein, 5 grams of fiber, and 100 milligrams of DHA omega-3s per package/serving. Each peel-and-eat package is one serving and weighs only 5.6 ounces.

It’s similar to other popular backpacking meals in both weight and nutrients per serving. But Wild Planet’s meals are ready to eat in seconds, no cooking or cold soaking required. In fact, you can bring four Wild Planet meals and still carry less than the weight of just one competing meal when combined with the weight of a typical lightweight stove, pot, and fuel. With all that weight savings, you can still add any crunchy toppings, sauces, and cheeses to boost your calorie count on big days. It’s an easy trail lunch that doesn’t compromise when it comes to flavor or nutrition.

It’s the combination of real, thoughtfully selected ingredients and no-prep convenience that sets Wild Planet’s meals apart. A lot of hikers go stoveless and resort to the bare essentials—“soaked quinoa plus whatever is on hand.” You can do better. When you hike with a Wild Tuna and Quinoa Bowl, you’ve got ingredients that are caught, grown, and chosen with intention. That means wild skipjack tuna, organic quinoa, delicious veggies, and gourmet spices, all sealed in organic extra virgin olive oil.

Hikers are naturally innovative, and with some thought, cold-soaking can deliver surprisingly elevated meals. If you want to try it for yourself, or want tips to supplement your ready-to-eat meals, here are a few basics:

Real ingredients are always a delicious luxury in the backcountry, even for the savviest of chefs. It’s one of the appeals of Wild Planet’s tuna bowls, especially for those new to stoveless backpacking. You can just pack and peel, then pair your summit views with wild-caught tuna, whole foods, and carefully crafted flavors.

As a hiker, you know the importance of low-impact practices. Wild Planet believes the same. The brand prioritizes sustainable fishing practices and ocean health, and uses only pole-and-line and troll fishing methods to catch its tuna. That means hauling in only one fish per line at a time; this selective fishing has benefits for the ocean and for you.

On the environmental side, these sustainable methods are focused on preventing two of the most damaging effects of the commercial fishing industry on ocean ecosystems—overfishing and bycatch. Overfishing depletes a fish population faster than it has the chance to repopulate. Bycatch, meanwhile, occurs when non-targeted species are hauled in by accident, like sharks, sea turtles, and marine mammals like dolphins. Wild Planet’s select fishing partners don’t use nets; they monitor closely for bycatch while reeling in one fish at a time.

#8169. Better for the Sea, Better for You

Canned seafood has long been a staple of the outdoor menu: It’s portable, nutritious, and adds a ton of flavor to simple meals. And it’s not just for hikers and campers. Canned and pouched seafood has been steadily rising in popularity in recent years, thanks in part to its protein, omega-3 fatty acids, and convenience. But while tuna can be a great choice for your health, how do you know if it’s a good choice for the environment?

Thanks to pioneering efforts to establish sustainable fishing practices—and make them transparent for consumers—it’s easier than ever to find options that support our complex marine ecosystems. Here’s why it matters.

According to the most recent data from the National Seafood Association, canned tuna is the third most popular seafood in the United States. That means a lot of tuna harvested from the world’s oceans, making harmful fishing practices even more harmful due to the enormity of the scale. This puts tuna and other fish populations at risk, and unfortunately, these practices still dominate the industry.

Purse seine fishing, which is responsible for about 66% of global tropical tuna catch, per the International Seafood Sustainability Foundation, can be harmful, especially when used in conjunction with fish aggregating devices (FADs). This method involves using a large wall of netting—up to 6,500 feet long and reaching around 650 feet in depth—to surround an entire school of fish. Non-selective mass fishing practices can deplete a population before it has a chance to properly reproduce, especially since it indiscriminately removes juvenile tuna from the ecosystem, threatening healthy repopulation.

Another key threat from large-scale industrial fishing is bycatch, or the unintentional harvesting of non-targeted species. Some of the species most impacted by the tuna industry include sharks, sea turtles, and marine mammals like dolphins. Net-based fishing with FADs is the most common culprit, since FADs don’t discriminate between which types of fish they attract. Bycatch also frequently occurs with longline fishing, which uses baited lines an average of 28 miles long. Animals caught as bycatch often do not survive.

How can things be done differently? Wild Planet is a case study. Since 2004, Wild Planet has focused on sourcing seafood through responsible fishing practices. Its wild albacore and skipjack tuna showcase how responsible fishing and high-quality products can—and should—go hand in hand.

All of Wild Planet’s tuna are caught individually using pole-and-line or trolling methods. Pole-and-line is exactly what it sounds like: one pole, one line, and one fish at a time. Trolling is similar, with multiple lines towed behind a slow-moving boat. Both the bait used and the speed at which the boat travels are specifically chosen to attract the targeted species. In both methods, fish are hauled in immediately, so non-targeted species can be quickly released.

The benefits of these inherently selective methods are twofold. First, they allow Wild Planet to specifically target tuna while minimizing bycatch of other marine species. Additionally, the company’s responsible fishing operations are able to further select what kind of tuna is being harvested. Wild Planet sources younger migratory tuna near the ocean’s surface, avoiding juvenile fish, who are key to repopulation efforts, and older, larger tuna that tend to accumulate higher levels of mercury. It’s an approach that’s better for you and the planet.

The Monterey Bay Aquarium Seafood Watch Program has a name for foods like this: Super Greens. It’s an exclusive list—it currently includes only 10 foods—that points to pole-and-line caught tuna as an option that’s high in omega-3s, low in mercury, and harvested with the ocean in mind.

The Monterey Bay Aquarium has a unique relationship with Wild Planet. The brand has not only been following the aquarium’s guidance since the beginning, but the institution is actually key to the company’s origin story. It was at a Monterey Bay Aquarium exhibit on fragile ocean ecosystems that Wild Planet founder Bill Carvalho was inspired to build a different kind of seafood company.

The Aquarium, in turn, is inspired by the efforts that many in the industry have taken in response to its suggestions. “Some of these companies have been with us from the very beginning,” Shawn Cronin, market engagement director for Seafood Watch said in 2024. “They make it easy for people to choose responsible seafood day-to-day, helping move the needle through their sourcing and by directly engaging in global improvement initiatives. It’s not an easy commitment to make.”

That emphasis on doing what’s right and trusting the science continues today. It’s the kind of thinking that guides the way Wild Planet fishes as well as the types of fish it sells. In addition to tuna, Wild Planet also sells mackerel, anchovies, and sardines. These smaller, lower-food-chain species can be more abundant and offer another responsibly sourced seafood option, while delivering plenty of protein, omega-3s, and flavor.

If you’re looking to incorporate more sustainable seafood into your life, the same principles extend beyond tuna. Always look for labels that call out pole-and-line caught, troll caught, and/or FAD-free fishing. Other information, like the specific species and where it was harvested, lets you know that the company knows—and cares—where its fish come from.

You can find out what sustainability tastes like for yourself. From now until December 22, Outside readers get 20% off everything on Wild Planet’s website with code OUTSIDE20. Because even though the impact of our choices might be harder to see when it’s an ocean away, it’s no less important.

Learn more at WildPlanetFoods.com.

In this economy, climbers can’t afford to pass up a good deal. Unless you’re crafty and have a sewing machine—not to mention a home welding kit—we imagine there are a few things you could use. Backcountry launched its Black Friday Sale early on November 20, with deals up to 60% off. We found some of the best deals on climbing shoes there. Competing outdoor retailer REI launched a Holiday Sale on November 13 with up to 25% off discounts that we expect to endure through Cyber Monday. However, if you’re shopping in person, keep in mind that the co-op is closed on Black Friday itself for its annual #OptOutside campaign.

On the brand side, Black Diamond has been running an outlet sale more or less all month with up to 50% off past styles (mostly apparel, but some hardgoods). Black Diamond is offering a Holiday Sale through November 30 with up to 25% off. On November 27, it shifts into deeper Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals of up to 60% off. We found some steals on editor-recommended gear at BD you won’t want to miss.

As you head into the discount madness, here are a couple Black Friday/Cyber Monday shopping tips for climbers:

Looking to build out your climbing shoe quiver? Is your go-to pair beyond the point of resole or repair? Ready to graduate to a more performance-oriented design? This is your moment. You may be thinking: But I’m not going to be climbing much for the next few months. I’ll just wait.

Real ones know that would be a grave error. Come February or March, you will still need new shoes. But chance are, they’ll be full price. Plus, if you plan ahead and invest now, you can spend the winter breaking them in around the gym. Here are a few standout Black Friday climbing deals on rock and approach shoes to consider below.

If your footwork repertoire involves pockets and micro edging, the La Sportiva Miura VS Climbing Shoe is among the best. Last year, we chose the Miura VS as the best tech shoe out there. With an aggressive downturn and semi-stiff, low-profile toe box, this shoe is perfect for precision climbing up slab and narrow cracks. Note that VS means this shoe uses a Velcro closure.

La Sportiva’s Katana is an awesome technical shoe for edging and beyond. Note that the men’s version is stiffer than the women’s version. This shoe is great for precision placements on slab, narrow cracks, and steep routes. After a buddy gifted me his slightly too small Katanas, I had them resoled and have been loving them indoors and out. You can also check out our review of the Katana here.

With great grip and breathability, these approach shoes strike a near-perfect balance between nimble hiking and climbing performance—without the weight. That’s why we selected the TX2 Evo as our top pick for a lightweight approach shoe last year. We also love that La Sportiva crafts this pair with recycled materials and a sole designed for easy repairs. This is one of the best Black Friday climbing deals out there if you need a good approach shoe.

We haven’t seen deals this pervasive on shoes in a while. All but ONE of the dozen pairs we gave top billing in our Fall 2026 Shoe Guide are marked down right now at Backcountry. (The only shoe that evaded discounts is the Scarpa Furia Air, our top pick for a “soft/high-feedback” shoe.) You can read our testers’ thoughts on each shoe in our guide, and see the deals on each shoe and what it’s best for below.

The Red Chili Voltage: “a sleeper classic—a tautly crafted, downturned, asymmetrical performance sport shoe with a solid crossover into bouldering.”

Scarpa VSR LV: “Across a range of styles and grades, testers praised the shoe’s precision on tiny footholds and its power on steep terrain.”

La Sportiva Ondra Comp: “Maybe the best toe-hooking shoe I have encountered—ever.”

Mad Rock D2 One: “… I can safely call these the most versatile, ideal for both bouldering and sport.”

Butora Ibex: “Hardcore boarders, boulderers, and comp climbers will love it, though I also found it versatile for vertical edging.”

Evolv Phantom Pro: “… offers big-time driving and grabbing power paired with a velvety, forgiving footbed and single-strap, sock-like closure.”

Ocún Jett S: “For a ‘narrow’ slipper, the Jett S still has enough lateral stretch to accommodate wide feet, with a comfy last great for long gym sessions—both bouldering and sport.”

La Sportiva Mantra: “With a big downcamber and mild asymmetry, the sensitive and pared-down Mantra is great for grabbing big, smeary holds.”

Evolv Zenist Pro: “The Zenist Pro stands out for its edging and all-around prowess, and is perhaps not as smeary or grabby as the marketing would have you believe.”

Scarpa Generator Mid: ““The Generator Mid’s big toe box was adept at rand smearing in a sustained corner crack and for the wide stuff, but boxy and insensitive in thin jams.”

Update: This shoe has sold out at Backcountry since we first published this deals round-up.

Scarpa Blackbird: “Over months of testing, the Blackbird has certainly lived up to its hype and its price … The edging power on the Blackbird is off the charts, with the best support and stability on square-cut edges of any shoe I’ve worn.”

Beyond shoes, there’s a lot more climbing gear on sale out there during Black Friday. Ropes, hardware, and more are all marked down 20% or more. Here are our top editor-tested picks.

Most climbers care about the planet. We can do our part in a lot of ways, one of which is buying more planet-friendly gear. Edelrid manufactured this 70m rope with over 40% renewable materials, leveraging a bio-based polyamide in part made from castor oil. This is the first synthetic rope of its kind that relies less heavily on fossil fuels. Of course, the rope has to work, too, and in tests, we found it held up well. It feeds well and proved kink-resistant in our tests. We dubbed it the best eco-friendly cord in our 2025 rope guide.

We tested Mammut’s Alpine Core Protect Rope and called it one of the safest ropes we’d ever used. It also held up remarkably well after significant abuse in the field. By weaving burly aramid fibers into its core, this innovative rope from Mammut helps resist cutting. And right now, you can snag it at 20% off.

Using the same cam-assisted blocking that makes the Grigri the safer choice over an ATC or other devices, the NEOX innovates with an integrated wheel that makes feeding out slack when lead belaying faster and smoother. Petzl also engineered the NEOX with recycled materials to reduce its environmental impact. We’ve used it for rock, gym, and ice climbing and we’re big fans.

I have been loving the Black Diamond Solution Hoody as a light fall belay jacket and even for cold rock climbing when I’m too chilly to shed my jacket. The Solution manages to be super lightweight, movement-friendly, and breathable, yet warm. This is largely because the specific PrimaLoft insulation used in this jacket is made with technology developed by NASA for astronauts. Here on earth, it also works great. It honestly does feel like being wrapped in warm air. The pocket real estate is also generous, and it’s nice that the whole thing packs into the left hand pocket so you can easily stash it in your pack.

A chance to save on cams? We’ll take it. Snag one (or a few) of this Black Diamond #.5 to enhance your rack for fast and light missions.

Our top all-around harness of Fall 2026, the Solution uses what Black Diamond dubs Contour Edge Technology for the waist and leg loops, meaning they’re more rigid in the middle, but flexible and soft at the edges for increased comfort. One of our testers found that this made for a climbing harness with “fantastic” hip support. It didn’t cause any uncomfortable pressure or distracting pain points on his body, steadfastly supporting him during 10-hour days on the wall.

One of our editors’ favorite gifts for this holiday season, Trango’s REAL Chalk is better for humans and the planet. This seawater-sourced chalk comes in 50g, 250g, or 500g bags. Makes for a great stocking stuffer—or stock up for yourself for 2027.

I bought a BD Momentum Full-Body Harness in 2018 or 2019 and am still using it today. It’s been through years of indoor and outdoor climbing with both of my kids. It’s user-friendly, too—a four-year-old can handle putting it on themselves. When my son finally outgrows his next spring, it’s in good enough shape that we will pass it down to another climbing family. This is a great time to save on a kids’ harness that will last until your kid outgrows it.

Perhaps the most hyped carabiner of 2026 (if there is such a thing as carabiner hype), the Magnetron returned by popular demand a few months ago. After quickly going out of stock, what’s been billed as “Alex Honnold’s favorite carabiner” is now back in inventory—and on sale. The biggest boon of this cult-favorite gear is that you can never forget to lock it, thanks to an automatic magnetic locking mechanism. However, it’s not great for ice/alpine climbing and can be a tad difficult to operate for smaller hand sizes. I personally have a small hand and find it easy to use and love it. But you can read our full thoughts here.

One of our top ice tool picks this winter, the Black Diamond Hydras offer an impeccably balanced swing, ultra-precise pick, and a high degree of modularity make the Black Diamond Hydra our tool of choice for moderate and vertical ice. Interchangeable screw-on head weights let us dial in balance for any terrain, and the razor-thin picks—2.5 millimeters at the tip versus a 3- to 3.5-millimeter industry average—place like a dream. Read more about the Hydras in our Winter Gear Guide.

Our best all-around helmet of Fall 2026, the Black Diamond Vision offers the best of both worlds when it comes to comfort and weight. Made from mostly foam, with a plastic, ABS hardshell covering a portion of the top of the helmet, the Vision is impressively light at 215 grams.

After quickly burning through Black Diamond Crack Gloves (that broke within a few months while climbing an indoor crack), I ordered a pair of these Ocún gloves a couple years ago and have loved them ever since. They are easy to put on, simple to clip to a back gear loop of your harness (I keep them clipped under my chalkbag), comfortable, and super durable on sandstone, granite, and human-made cracks alike.

#8167. A Hiker Died Along the PCT After Winter Ice Turned a Popular Trail Dangerous

Snow covers the slopes of Southern California's San Gabriel Mountains, where a hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet on Mount Baden-Powell (Photo: Noah Sauve/Getty Images)

A hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet while trying to help his son on Mount Baden-Powell, a 9,399-foot peak in Southern California’s San Gabriel Mountains, according to a GoFundMe organized by the hiker’s niece.

The GoFundMe page identified the man as Guillermo Alejandro Batres. His niece, Jennifer Morse, wrote on the fundraising page that Batres and his son were attempting to summit the mountain when the younger man slipped and fell. When Batres tried to help him up, he lost his footing and fell down a steep gulch.

“On this mountain, there’s no room for error if you slip when it’s snowy or icy out,” Cris Hazzard, a Southern California hiking expert who has climbed Baden-Powell dozens of times, told Outside. “If you slip in the summer, you probably just fall on your butt, maybe go down some gravel. You slip in the winter, you’re going down hundreds, if not thousands, of feet.”

AV Scanner News, a local outlet that monitors emergency dispatches, reported that authorities received a call about the incident around 10:09 A.M. after the hikers encountered snow and ice roughly three miles from the Vincent Gap trailhead. Los Angeles County firefighters and sheriff’s deputies responded near mile marker 71 on Angeles Crest Highway. Authorities also requested the sheriff’s department’s Air Rescue 5 helicopter crew to recover Batres’s body, according to the outlet.

Authorities have not independently confirmed the family’s account of the fall, and the sheriff’s department did not respond to Outside‘s request for comment before publication.

Located in Angeles National Forest northeast of Los Angeles, Baden-Powell is a popular warm-weather climb. The standard summit route begins at Vincent Gap, a 6,585-foot mountain pass along Angeles Crest Highway. From there, hikers follow the Pacific Crest Trail for roughly four miles, climbing more than 2,800 feet through 35 wooded switchbacks up the mountain’s north face before reaching an exposed ridge near the summit.

Because the mountain’s north-facing slopes receive less direct sunlight, snow tends to linger there, Hazzard told Outside. During warmer days, that snow can melt and refreeze overnight, leaving patches of ice along the trail. Although the San Gabriel Mountains receive snow every winter, the conditions can catch visitors off guard so close to Los Angeles.

Batres had hiked Baden-Powell at least once before, according to the GoFundMe, and Hazzard noted that even experienced hikers face heightened risk once ice forms on the route.

“If you are experienced and you know the dangers, there’s still a higher risk of something going wrong than there would be without that snow or ice, regardless of how careful you are,” Hazzard said. “Each winter, we get people going up there who don’t really understand that the hike they did in the summer is now a mountaineering exercise. It’s so steep, and there are dangerous runouts. If you slip, you might hit your head. There’s a lot you can bang into on the way down.”

Batres’s death occurred just two days after another hiker survived a serious fall on the same mountain. In a November 21 statement on X, the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department described rescuing a hiker who had slid more than 300 feet down a snowy chute on Baden-Powell on November 20.

Responders initially struggled to locate the person due to inaccurate GPS coordinates, completing the rescue shortly before worsening weather would have grounded the helicopter.

Similar falls have occurred in past winters. In February 2016, a 69-year-old hiker slid roughly 100 feet down an icy chute before a sheriff’s helicopter airlifted him to a trauma center. Nearby Mount Baldy has also experienced deadly winter accidents, including three hiking fatalities in the first week of January 2026.

Despite having climbed Baden-Powell in winter with experienced mountaineers using crampons, Hazzard said he now avoids the peak once snow arrives. Instead, he recommends seeking formal mountaineering training before attempting snow-covered summits or choosing lower-elevation desert trails around Joshua Tree and Palm Springs.

“They shouldn’t do it in the winter,” Hazzard said. “But winter is the great time to go and do the hikes you can’t safely do in summer, and leave the high peaks alone.”
